name: ChildProcess
comment:
A program sometimes needs another program to do part of its work, and this module starts
one. A program started by the running program is its _child process_, or _child_.

There are two ways to start a child, and they differ in how its input, its output and its end
reach the program.

[`run`](#run) is a `Task` that waits for the child to end. The child's standard input is empty.
Everything it writes to its standard output and standard error is collected, up to a limit, and
handed over when it ends: as a [`SuccessfulRun`](#SuccessfulRun) when it exits with code 0
within its limits, and otherwise as a [`FailedRun`](#FailedRun).

[`spawn`](#spawn) is a `Cmd` that starts the child and lets it run alongside the program. Two
messages report on it: the [`Connection`](#Connection) message once it has started (or failed
to start), and the `onExit` message, with its exit code, once it has ended. The connection
decides what the child's standard input, output and error are: the program's own, new streams
handed to the program ([`StreamIO`](#StreamIO)), or the null device. A spawned child is identified
by a `Process.Id`: an Elm process that stands for the child until it exits. Until it exits, a
spawned child keeps the program running, unless it is `Detached`, as [`Connection`](#Connection)
describes ([`System`](System) describes when a program ends).

Three facts hold for both.

The program and its arguments reach the child unchanged only with the `NoShell`
[`Shell`](#Shell). The default shell, which both [`defaultRunOptions`](#defaultRunOptions) and
[`defaultSpawnOptions`](#defaultSpawnOptions) use, joins them with single spaces and no quoting
into one command line for `/bin/sh` (`%ComSpec%` on the native backend under Windows), so
spaces, quotes, globs and other shell syntax in an argument are interpreted by the shell. Under a
shell, a program that cannot be found is reported by the shell's exit code, not as a failure to
start.

The only signal this module sends is `SIGTERM`. It is sent, to a child that has not yet exited,
when a [`RunDuration`](#RunDuration) expires, when a `run` child writes more than its output limit,
and when `Process.kill` is called on a `run` task or on a spawned child's `Process.Id`. It goes to
the process that was started, which under a shell may be the shell rather than the program.

The two report exit codes differently. `run` reports a child that died from a signal, or that
reached one of its limits, as exit code `-1`. `spawn`'s `onExit` reports a death from signal
number `n` as `128 + n`, and a child that could not be started at all as a negative number
(`-2` for `ENOENT` on Linux and macOS).

unions.name: Connection
unions.comment:
How a spawned child's standard input, output and error are connected, together with the
message that reports its start.

Each constructor holds the function that makes that message. It is given a `Process.Id` for an
Elm process that stands for the child until the child exits; it is not the operating system's
process id. `Process.kill` on it sends the child `SIGTERM` if it has not yet exited, and the
`onExit` message still arrives when the child ends.

`Integrated` gives the child the running program's own standard input, output and error.

`External` gives the child three new pipes, and hands the program the other ends as a
[`StreamIO`](#StreamIO) alongside the `Process.Id`. When the child could not be started, the
message still arrives, and its streams are connected to no program.

`Ignored` connects the child's standard input, output and error to the null device: it reads the
end of input at once, and what it writes is discarded.

`Detached` is `Ignored` with the child in a new session. Unlike the others, a detached child does
not keep the program running, so the program can end while the child still runs. A detached
child with a `runDuration` does keep the program running, until the limit expires or the child
exits.

unions.name: EnvironmentVariables
unions.comment:
The environment variables the child starts with.

`InheritEnvironmentVariables` gives it the running program's variables.

`MergeWithEnvironmentVariables` gives it the running program's variables together with those in
the `Dict`; a variable in both takes the `Dict`'s value.

`ReplaceEnvironmentVariables` gives it the variables in the `Dict` and no others.

unions.name: FailedRun
unions.comment:
Why a [`run`](#run) did not succeed: the child could not be started, or it was started and
did not succeed.

`InitError` means that no child was started. `program` and `arguments` are those given to
`run`, and `error` says why the child could not be started, as a [`StartError`](#StartError).
Under a shell, the shell is what is started, so a program the shell cannot find is a `ProgramError`
with the shell's exit code, not an `InitError`.

`ProgramError` means that the child ran. `exitCode` is `-1` when the child died from a signal,
and when it reached `runDuration` or `maximumBytesWrittenToStreams`, whatever exit code it then
ended with. Otherwise it is the child's non-zero exit code. `stdout` and `stderr` hold the output
collected from the child, each cut at `maximumBytesWrittenToStreams`. Once a limit has stopped the
run, output not yet read when the child exited is dropped. On the native backend under Windows,
`exitCode` is always `-1` and no output is collected, as [`run`](#run) says.
cases: { program : String.String, arguments : List.List String.String, error : ChildProcess.StartError }
{ exitCode : Basics.Int, stdout : Bytes.Bytes, stderr : Bytes.Bytes }

unions.name: RunDuration
unions.comment:
How long the child may run before it is sent `SIGTERM`.

`Milliseconds` counts from the moment the child is started. A value of 0 or less is the same as
`NoLimit`.

When the limit expires, a [`run`](#run) fails with `exitCode` `-1`, while a [`spawn`](#spawn)'s
`onExit` gets whatever exit code the child then ends with.

unions.name: Shell
unions.comment:
How the program and its arguments are turned into the process that is started.

`NoShell` starts the program itself, and passes it each argument exactly as given.

`DefaultShell` joins the program and its arguments into one command line, separated by single
spaces and with no quoting, and starts `/bin/sh -c` with that line. The shell splits the line
again by its own rules, so an argument holding a space becomes two, and quotes, globs, variables
and other shell syntax take effect. It is the shell that is started, so a program it cannot find
is reported by the shell's exit code.

`CustomShell` does the same with the named shell in place of `/bin/sh`. An empty name means the
same shell as `DefaultShell`.

On the native backend under Windows, the default shell is `%ComSpec%` (usually `cmd.exe`), and
both shells are given `/d /s /c` in place of `-c`.

unions.name: StartError
unions.comment:
Why a [`run`](#run) could not start its child, as reported by the operating system when it
tried to start the program. The system error each case stands for is given in parentheses.

`ProgramNotFound` means that no program exists at the given name or path, or that it could not
be found on the search path (`ENOENT`).

`PermissionDenied` means that the program exists but may not be run: it is not executable, or a
directory on the way to it cannot be searched (`EACCES`).

`NotExecutable` means that the file is not in a format the operating system can run (`ENOEXEC`).

`ArgumentsTooLong` means that the arguments, together with the environment variables, are larger
than the operating system accepts (`E2BIG`).

`ProcessLimitReached` means that the system or the user is out of the resources a new process
needs: too many processes, too little memory, or too many open files (`EAGAIN`, `ENOMEM`,
`EMFILE`, `ENFILE`).

`OtherStartError` holds the name of any other system error, as the operating system or backend
reported it, for example `"ENOTDIR"`.

Under a shell, the shell is what is started, so these describe the shell; a program the shell
cannot start is a `ProgramError` with the shell's exit code instead.

unions.name: WorkingDirectory
unions.comment:
The directory the child starts in.

`InheritWorkingDirectory` is the running program's current directory. `SetWorkingDirectory`
names another. Neither changes the running program's own directory.

aliases.name: RunOptions
aliases.comment:
The options of [`run`](#run): how the child is started, and the limits on it.

`maximumBytesWrittenToStreams` limits standard output and standard error separately. When the
child writes more than that to either, it is sent `SIGTERM` if it is still running, and the run
fails with a `ProgramError` whose `exitCode` is `-1`, holding the output collected so far cut at
the limit. A value of 0 or less means no limit.
aliases.type: { shell : ChildProcess.Shell, workingDirectory : ChildProcess.WorkingDirectory, environmentVariables : ChildProcess.EnvironmentVariables, maximumBytesWrittenToStreams : Basics.Int, runDuration : ChildProcess.RunDuration }

aliases.name: SpawnOptions
aliases.comment:
The options of [`spawn`](#spawn): how the child is started, how it is connected to the
program, and the message that reports its end.

`onExit` makes the message from the child's exit code. That is the child's own code when it
exits, `128 + n` when it dies from signal number `n`, and a negative number when it could not
be started: on Linux and macOS, minus the system error number (`-2` for `ENOENT`), and `-1` for a
failure that has no error number.
aliases.type: { shell : ChildProcess.Shell, workingDirectory : ChildProcess.WorkingDirectory, environmentVariables : ChildProcess.EnvironmentVariables, runDuration : ChildProcess.RunDuration, connection : ChildProcess.Connection msg, onExit : Basics.Int -> msg }

aliases.name: StreamIO
aliases.comment:
The three streams of a child spawned with `External`. `stdin` writes to the child's
standard input; `stdout` and `stderr` read what it writes to its standard output and standard
error. A failure on one of them arrives as a `Stream.Error`, as [`Stream`](Stream) describes:
when a pipe itself fails, the operation fails with `Stream.Failed`, and
[`Stream.failureToString`](Stream#failureToString) describes the problem.
aliases.type: { stdin : Stream.Writable Bytes.Bytes, stdout : Stream.Readable Bytes.Bytes, stderr : Stream.Readable Bytes.Bytes }

aliases.name: SuccessfulRun
aliases.comment:
What a [`run`](#run) that succeeded hands over: everything the child wrote to its standard
output and standard error. A run succeeds when the child exits with code 0 and reaches neither
limit of its [`RunOptions`](#RunOptions).
aliases.type: { stdout : Bytes.Bytes, stderr : Bytes.Bytes }

values.name: defaultRunOptions
values.comment:
A starting set of options for [`run`](#run): the default shell, the running program's
working directory and environment variables, at most 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) on each of
standard output and standard error, and no time limit.

values.name: defaultSpawnOptions
values.comment:
Builds [`spawn`](#spawn) options from `connection` and `onExit`, with the
default shell, the running program's working directory and environment variables, and no time
limit.

values.name: run
values.comment:
Starts `program` with `arguments`, as `options` say, and waits for it to end.

    ChildProcess.run "cat" [ "my_file" ] ChildProcess.defaultRunOptions

The task succeeds with a [`SuccessfulRun`](#SuccessfulRun) when the child exits with code 0
within both limits of `options`, and fails with a [`FailedRun`](#FailedRun) otherwise. The
child's standard input is the null device, so it reads the end of input at once.

The task ends only once the child has exited and, unless one of the limits of `options` has
stopped the run, its standard output and standard error have both reached their end. A process the
child started that keeps them open therefore delays the result until `runDuration` expires; the run
then fails with `exitCode` `-1` and the output collected so far.

Killing the task with `Process.kill` sends the child `SIGTERM` if it is still running, and the
task then never completes.

On the native backend under Windows, the output is not collected, and every run that starts a
child fails with `exitCode` `-1`.
values.type: String.String -> List.List String.String -> ChildProcess.RunOptions -> Task.Task ChildProcess.FailedRun ChildProcess.SuccessfulRun

values.name: spawn
values.comment:
Starts `program` with `arguments`, as `options` say, and lets it run alongside the program.

    ChildProcess.spawn "tail" [ "-f", "my_file" ] mySpawnOptions

The `connection` message arrives once the child has started, and the `onExit` message once it
has ended. When the program cannot be started at all, both still arrive: the `connection`
message first, then `onExit` with a negative number (`-2` when the program does not exist, on
Linux and macOS). Under a shell, a program the shell cannot find is reported by the shell's exit
code instead.

On the native backend under Windows, `spawn` stops the program with a fatal error.
values.type: String.String -> List.List String.String -> ChildProcess.SpawnOptions msg -> Platform.Cmd.Cmd msg

name: FileSystem
comment:
A program needs to read, write and manage the files, directories and links it names, and this
module does that by [Path](Path#Path). Apart from the file streams, each task here opens and
closes whatever it needs. To keep a file open, read and write it at offsets, or act on the file
that was opened even after its path has been renamed or replaced, use
[FileSystem.Handle](FileSystem-Handle).

An _entity_ is anything a path can name: a file, a directory, a symbolic link, a socket, a device
or a pipe (see [EntityType](#EntityType)).

A path reaches the operating system as the text [Path.toPosixString](Path#toPosixString) prints,
and every path that comes back, from [realPath](#realPath), [readLink](#readLink),
[listDirectory](#listDirectory), [makeTempDirectory](#makeTempDirectory), the special paths and
watch events, is parsed with [Path.fromPosixString](Path#fromPosixString). Both are lexical and
lossy, as the [Path](Path) module describes.

Most functions that change the file system succeed with a `Path`, so that calls on one entity can
be chained. It is the path the function was given, with two exceptions. The two-path functions
[move](#move), [copyFile](#copyFile), [hardLink](#hardLink) and [softLink](#softLink) take the
destination, or the new link, first and the source, or the target, second, and succeed with the
first. [makeTempDirectory](#makeTempDirectory) succeeds with the directory it created.
[writeFileStream](#writeFileStream) and [writeFileStreamWith](#writeFileStreamWith) succeed with
a stream instead.

A task here that fails, fails with an [Error](#Error), which carries the path it concerns, the
kind of failure ([ErrorKind](#ErrorKind)) and a message. For the two-path functions that path is
the first one as well; [errorPath](#errorPath) gives the full rule.

[readFileStream](#readFileStream) and [writeFileStream](#writeFileStream) hand the file over as
a stream. They open the file before the task succeeds, so a file that cannot be opened fails the
task with an `Error`. After that, a failure of the file arrives on the stream as
`Stream.Failed`, and [fromStreamFailure](#fromStreamFailure) reads it back as an `Error`, as the
[Stream](Stream) module describes.

Two kinds of write ask more than [writeFile](#writeFile) gives, and [WriteOptions](#WriteOptions)
selects them. A _durable_ write flushes the file's data to the storage device before it
succeeds. An _exclusive_ write creates the file, and fails if anything already exists at the
path.

[watch](#watch) and [watchRecursive](#watchRecursive) are subscriptions to changes at a path.
While a subscription to a path that could be watched exists, it keeps the program running.

On the native backend under Windows the file system is not supported: every task here that can
fail fails with [NotSupported](#ErrorKind), and a watch subscription stops the program with a
fatal error.

unions.name: AccessPermission
unions.comment:
One way of accessing an entity: reading it, writing it, or executing it.

[checkAccess](#checkAccess) tests a list of them, and [changeAccess](#changeAccess) grants a
list of them to each of an entity's owner, group and everyone else.

unions.name: EntityType
unions.comment:
The kind of an entity in the file system.

`File` is a regular file. `Socket` is a Unix domain socket. `Symlink` is a symbolic link, which is
reported only where a link is not followed: by [metadata](#metadata) with `resolveLink = False`,
and by [listDirectory](#listDirectory). `Device` is a character or block device, or any other
kind of entity not named here. `Pipe` is a named pipe (FIFO).

unions.name: ErrorKind
unions.comment:
What kind of failure an [Error](#Error) is.

Each kind names what went wrong rather than how the operating system spelled it. The codes in
parentheses are the ones each kind stands for, errno names except where noted; they are what
`errorToString` mentions and what a search of the operating system's documentation finds.

  - `NoSuchFileOrDirectory` (`ENOENT`): the entity, or a directory on its path, does not exist.
  - `FileExists` (`EEXIST`): something already exists at a path that had to be new, as for an
    exclusive write (see [WriteOptions](#WriteOptions)), a link path that is taken, or a
    non-recursive [makeDirectory](#makeDirectory) of a directory that exists.
  - `DirectoryFound` (`EISDIR`): a directory was found where a file was needed, as when
    [readFile](#readFile), [readFileStream](#readFileStream) or [copyFile](#copyFile) is given a
    directory.
  - `DirectoryRemoveNotRecursive` (Node's `ERR_FS_EISDIR`): a [remove](#remove) with
    `recursive = False` was given a directory. It is a separate kind from `DirectoryFound`,
    because removing the directory is possible: with `recursive = True`.
  - `NotADirectory` (`ENOTDIR`): an entry that had to be a directory, either the path itself or
    an entry on it, is something else.
  - `DirectoryNotEmpty` (`ENOTEMPTY`): a directory that had to be empty is not.
  - `PermissionDenied` (`EACCES`): access permissions, of the entity or of a directory on its
    path, refused the operation.
  - `NotPermitted` (`EPERM`): the operation needs a privilege the program does not have, such as
    changing the owner of a file it does not own.
  - `TooManyOpenFiles` (`EMFILE`, `ENFILE`): the program, or the whole system, has as many files
    open as it is allowed.
  - `LinkLoop` (`ELOOP`): resolving the path followed too many symbolic links, as happens when
    links form a loop.
  - `PathTooLong` (`ENAMETOOLONG`): the path, or an entry on it, is too long.
  - `InvalidInput` (`EINVAL`): an argument was not valid for the operation, as when
    [readLink](#readLink) is given a path that is not a symbolic link.
  - `IOError` (`EIO`): a low-level input or output error, such as a failing storage device.
  - `NotSupported` (`ENOTSUP`, `EOPNOTSUPP`): the operation is not supported here, as for every
    task of this module on the native backend under Windows.
  - `CrossDevice` (`EXDEV`): the operation cannot cross from one file system to another, as when
    [move](#move) is given paths on two different file systems.
  - `HandleClosed` (`EBADF`): a [FileSystem.Handle](FileSystem-Handle) was used after it was
    closed.
  - `NoSpace` (`ENOSPC`, `EDQUOT`): the storage device is full, or the user's quota is used up.
  - `ReadOnlyFileSystem` (`EROFS`): the operation would change a file system that is mounted
    read-only.
  - `OtherFileSystemError code` is any other failure, with the code as the backend reported it,
    such as `"EBUSY"`. The two backends do not always report the same code for the same
    failure, so a program should not depend on the text.

unions.name: ReadFileStreamMode
unions.comment:
Which bytes of a file [readFileStream](#readFileStream) delivers. Offsets count bytes from the
beginning of the file.

`Beginning` delivers the whole file.

`From n` skips the first `n` bytes and delivers the rest. A negative `n` is 0, and an `n` past the
end gives a stream with nothing in it.

`Between` delivers the bytes from `start` to `end`, and `end` is **inclusive**:
`Between { start = 0, end = 9 }` delivers ten bytes, or fewer if the file is shorter. A negative
`start` is 0. A negative `end` delivers everything from `start` to the end of the file; otherwise
an `end` before `start` delivers nothing.

unions.name: WatchEvent
unions.comment:
A change seen by [watch](#watch) or [watchRecursive](#watchRecursive).

`Changed` means an entity's contents or attributes changed, such as a write to a file or a change
of its permissions.

`Moved` means an entity was created, deleted or renamed. A rename is usually two `Moved` events,
one for the old name and one for the new. On the JS backend under Linux, a change to a
directory's attributes is also reported as `Moved`.

An event about another entity carries that entity's path, relative to the watched path (on the JS
backend, when Node.js reports one). An event about the watched path itself carries `Nothing` on
the native backend; on the JS backend it can carry the watched entry's own name instead, so a
change to a watched file `f.txt` carries the path `f.txt`.

unions.name: WriteFileStreamMode
unions.comment:
Where the bytes written to a [writeFileStream](#writeFileStream) go in the file.

`Replace` empties the file, or creates it, and writes from the beginning.

`ReplaceFrom n` keeps the first `n` bytes and writes from there. A file shorter than `n` is
extended with zero bytes up to `n` once anything is written or the stream is closed. When the stream is closed, the file is cut off
where the writing ended, so whatever followed is gone; a cancelled stream is not cut off. For
`n > 0` the file must already exist, unless `createNew` (see [WriteOptions](#WriteOptions)) is set, which
requires that it does not and creates it.
`ReplaceFrom n` with `n <= 0` is `Replace`, and creates the file.

`Append` writes at the end of the file, creating it if it does not exist.

aliases.name: Error
aliases.comment:
A failed file system operation: the path it concerned, the kind of failure, and a message
describing it.

The three parts are read with [errorPath](#errorPath), [errorKind](#errorKind) and
[errorToString](#errorToString). Which kind a failure gets can depend on the operating system. An
`Error` is not interchangeable with `Socket.Error` or `Stream.Error`. Only the tasks of this
module and of [FileSystem.Handle](FileSystem-Handle) make one, and
[fromStreamFailure](#fromStreamFailure) reads one back from a file stream's failure.
aliases.type: FileSystem.Internal.Error

aliases.name: Metadata
aliases.comment:
What the operating system reports about one entity, as [metadata](#metadata) returns it.

`deviceID` identifies the device that holds the entity; for a `Device` entity it is not the
number of the device the entity stands for. `userID` and `groupID` are the owner's numeric ids.
`blockSize` is the size in bytes the operating system prefers for IO, and `blocks` is the number
of blocks allocated to the entity, which Linux and macOS count in 512-byte units, not in units of
`blockSize`.

The four times are whole milliseconds. `lastChanged` is the status change time, when the entity's
metadata or contents last changed, not a creation time. `created` is the time the entity was
created when that can be read (natively, on macOS, and on Linux when `statx` reports one; on the
JS backend, when Node.js reports one); otherwise it is the status change time, equal to
`lastChanged`.
aliases.type: { entityType : FileSystem.EntityType, deviceID : Basics.Int, userID : Basics.Int, groupID : Basics.Int, byteSize : Basics.Int, blockSize : Basics.Int, blocks : Basics.Int, lastAccessed : Time.Posix, lastModified : Time.Posix, lastChanged : Time.Posix, created : Time.Posix }

aliases.name: WriteOptions
aliases.comment:
What [writeFileWith](#writeFileWith) and [writeFileStreamWith](#writeFileStreamWith) ask of a
write beyond what [writeFile](#writeFile) does.

`createNew` makes the write exclusive. The file is created, and the task fails with
[FileExists](#ErrorKind) if anything already exists at the path. The operating
system checks and creates in one step (`O_EXCL`), so of two programs creating the same file at
most one succeeds.

`sync` makes the write durable. The file's data is flushed to the storage device (`fsync`) before
the write succeeds; for [writeFileStreamWith](#writeFileStreamWith), before closing the stream
succeeds.

Neither replaces a file in one step. Without `createNew`, [writeFileWith](#writeFileWith) empties
an existing file before writing, so a failure part way leaves it empty or partly written. To
replace a file in one step, write a new file with `sync` and [move](#move) it over the old one.
aliases.type: { createNew : Basics.Bool, sync : Basics.Bool }

values.name: accessPermissionsToInt
values.comment:
Returns the POSIX permission digit for a list of permissions: 4 for `Read`, plus 2 for
`Write`, plus 1 for `Execute`. A permission listed twice counts once.

    accessPermissionsToInt [ Read, Write ] == 6

values.name: appendToFile
values.comment: Adds the bytes to the end of the file at the path, creating the file if it does not exist.

values.name: changeAccess
values.comment:
Sets the access permissions of the entity at the path, for its owner, its group and everyone
else.

Each list becomes one octal digit of the file mode, as
[accessPermissionsToInt](#accessPermissionsToInt) computes it, so
`{ owner = [ Read, Write ], group = [ Read ], others = [ Read ] }` sets the mode `644`. The mode
has no other bits, so the set-user-ID, set-group-ID and sticky bits are cleared.
values.type: { owner : List.List FileSystem.AccessPermission, group : List.List FileSystem.AccessPermission, others : List.List FileSystem.AccessPermission } -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error Path.Path

values.name: changeOwner
values.comment:
Sets the user and group that own the entity at the path, given as numeric ids.

With `resolveLink = False` the owner of a symbolic link itself is changed, not that of the
entity it points to.
values.type: { userID : Basics.Int, groupID : Basics.Int, resolveLink : Basics.Bool } -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error Path.Path

values.name: changeTimes
values.comment:
Sets the last access and last modification times of the entity at the path.

The times are set in whole seconds: each is sent as its milliseconds divided by 1000 with `//`,
which rounds down for times after 1970 and toward zero for times before. On the JS backend `//`
gives a 32-bit result, so a time from 2038-01-19T03:14:08Z on, or at or before
1901-12-13T20:45:51Z, is not set as given.

With `resolveLink = False` the times of a symbolic link itself are changed, not those of the
entity it points to.
values.type: { lastAccessed : Time.Posix, lastModified : Time.Posix, resolveLink : Basics.Bool } -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error Path.Path

values.name: checkAccess
values.comment:
Checks that the program may access the entity at the path in each of the given ways, and
succeeds with the path if it may.

An empty list checks only that the entity exists.
values.type: List.List FileSystem.AccessPermission -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error Path.Path

values.name: copyFile
values.comment:
Copies the file at the second path to the first.

    copyFile destinationPath sourcePath

An existing file at the destination is overwritten, and the copy gets the source's mode. A
directory as the source fails with [DirectoryFound](#ErrorKind) before the destination is touched. The task
succeeds with the destination path, and if it fails, [errorPath](#errorPath) is the destination
path.

values.name: currentWorkingDirectory
values.comment:
The program's current working directory, which the operating system resolves relative paths
against. It is [Path.empty](Path#empty) if the directory cannot be read.

values.name: defaultWriteOptions
values.comment:
Write options with both `createNew` and `sync` off, which give the behaviour of
[writeFile](#writeFile) and [writeFileStream](#writeFileStream).

values.name: devNull
values.comment:
The path of the null device, `/dev/null`, which reads as empty and discards whatever is
written to it.

On Windows the kernels report `//./nul`, which [Path.fromPosixString](Path#fromPosixString)
parses into `/nul`, a path that does not name the null device.

values.name: errorKind
values.comment:
Returns the kind of failure an error is.

    case FileSystem.errorKind error of
        FileSystem.NoSuchFileOrDirectory ->
            Task.succeed defaultConfig

        _ ->
            Task.fail error

values.name: errorPath
values.comment:
Returns the path an error concerns.

For a function of this module it is the path the function was given, with two exceptions. For
[move](#move), [copyFile](#copyFile), [hardLink](#hardLink) and [softLink](#softLink) it is the
first path, the destination or new link, even when the failure was about the source. For
[makeTempDirectory](#makeTempDirectory) it is [tempDirectory](#tempDirectory) with the prefix
appended, without the random characters, which is not the path of any directory it created.

For an operation on an open [FileSystem.Handle](FileSystem-Handle) it is
[Path.empty](Path#empty), and so is it for an error read back by
[fromStreamFailure](#fromStreamFailure).

values.name: errorToString
values.comment:
Returns the error's message as the kernel gave it, with no path added.

The message usually begins with the operating system's code for the failure, as in
`"ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/x'"`. The message for a
[DirectoryRemoveNotRecursive](#ErrorKind) failure does not: it is
`"Path is a directory: rm returned EISDIR (is a directory) /x"`.

values.name: fromStreamFailure
values.comment:
Reads back the failure of a file stream as an `Error`, or returns `Nothing` for a failure that
a stream of this module did not report.

A stream from [readFileStream](#readFileStream), [writeFileStream](#writeFileStream) or
[writeFileStreamWith](#writeFileStreamWith) that fails because of its file, for example a read
error from a failing device or a write to a full one, fails a read or write with
`Stream.Failed failure`:

    case streamError of
        Stream.Failed failure ->
            case FileSystem.fromStreamFailure failure of
                Just error ->
                    -- FileSystem.errorKind error is, for example, FileSystem.NoSpace
                    reportFileError error

                Nothing ->
                    reportOther (Stream.failureToString failure)

        _ ->
            reportOther (Stream.errorToString streamError)

The error's [errorPath](#errorPath) is [Path.empty](Path#empty): the stream does not carry its
file's path.

values.name: hardLink
values.comment:
Creates a hard link at the first path to the file at the second.

    hardLink linkPath targetPath

A hard link is a second name for the same file, and neither name is the original. The task
succeeds with the link path, and if it fails, [errorPath](#errorPath) is the link path.

values.name: homeDirectory
values.comment:
The home directory of the current user.

It is `$HOME` when that is set and not empty, otherwise the home directory recorded for the user
in the system's user database (natively on Windows, `%USERPROFILE%`), and
[Path.empty](Path#empty) when there is none.

values.name: listDirectory
values.comment:
Returns the entries of the directory at the path, without `.` and `..`, sorted by name byte by
byte (as UTF-8).

Each `path` is the entry's name alone, relative to the listed directory, parsed with
[Path.fromPosixString](Path#fromPosixString). A name that parsing changes, such as `a.`, which
comes back as `a`, therefore does not name its entry once appended to the directory's path.

Each `entityType` is that of the entry itself: a symbolic link is `Symlink`, not followed.
values.type: Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (List.List { path : Path.Path, entityType : FileSystem.EntityType })

values.name: makeDirectory
values.comment:
Creates a directory at the path.

With `recursive = False` the parent directory must exist, and the task fails with [FileExists](#ErrorKind)
if something is already at the path. With `recursive = True` every missing directory on the path is
created too, and a directory already at the path is not an error.
values.type: { recursive : Basics.Bool } -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error Path.Path

values.name: makeTempDirectory
values.comment:
Creates a new directory in [tempDirectory](#tempDirectory), named `prefix` followed by six
random characters, and succeeds with its path. Each call creates a different directory.

If it fails, [errorPath](#errorPath) is [tempDirectory](#tempDirectory) with `prefix` appended,
without the random characters.

values.name: metadata
values.comment:
Returns the metadata of the entity at the path.

With `resolveLink = True` a symbolic link is followed and the entity it points to is described.
With `resolveLink = False` a link is described itself, with the `entityType` `Symlink`.
values.type: { resolveLink : Basics.Bool } -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error FileSystem.Metadata

values.name: move
values.comment:
Moves, or renames, the entity at the second path to the first.

    move newPath oldPath

The task succeeds with the new path. If it fails, [errorPath](#errorPath) is the new path. This
is the operating system's rename and nothing more, so a move to another file system fails
with [CrossDevice](#ErrorKind) rather than copying.

values.name: readFile
values.comment:
Reads the whole of the file at the path.

The contents are read into memory at once. For a very large file,
[readFileStream](#readFileStream) reads it in pieces instead.

values.name: readFileStream
values.comment:
Opens the file at the path and returns a stream of its bytes, the ones `mode` selects.

The file is opened before the task succeeds, so a file that cannot be opened, such as a missing
file ([NoSuchFileOrDirectory](#ErrorKind)) or a directory ([DirectoryFound](#ErrorKind)), fails
this task with an [Error](#Error). A failure of the file while reading arrives on the stream as
`Stream.Failed`, which [fromStreamFailure](#fromStreamFailure) reads back as an `Error`.

values.name: readLink
values.comment:
Returns the path stored in the soft link at the path.

The stored text is parsed with [Path.fromPosixString](Path#fromPosixString), so the result may
not print back as the stored text. It is not resolved against the link's directory.

values.name: realPath
values.comment:
Returns the path the operating system gives for the entity at the path, with every symbolic
link resolved. The entity must exist.

values.name: remove
values.comment:
Removes the entity at the path.

A symbolic link is removed itself, not the entity it points to. A directory is removed only with
`recursive = True`, and then together with everything in it. With `recursive = False` it fails
with [DirectoryRemoveNotRecursive](#ErrorKind), not [DirectoryFound](#ErrorKind).
values.type: { recursive : Basics.Bool } -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error Path.Path

values.name: softLink
values.comment:
Creates a soft link at the first path that points to the second.

    softLink linkPath targetPath

A soft link, also called a symbolic link, is a special file holding the path of another
location, which is followed when the link is resolved. The target is stored as the text
[Path.toPosixString](Path#toPosixString) prints and is not checked, so it need not exist. The
task succeeds with the link path, and if it fails, [errorPath](#errorPath) is the link path.

values.name: tempDirectory
values.comment:
The directory meant for temporary files.

It is the first of the `TMPDIR`, `TMP` and `TEMP` environment variables that is set and not
empty, and otherwise `/tmp` (`C:/Windows/Temp` on Windows).

values.name: truncateFile
values.comment:
Sets the length of the file at the path, in bytes: a longer file loses the bytes past
`length`, and a shorter one is extended with zero bytes. The file must already exist.

values.name: unlink
values.comment:
Removes the name at the path, which may name anything but a directory. A soft link is removed
itself, not the entity it points to; [remove](#remove) removes a directory.

values.name: watch
values.comment:
Creates a subscription to the changes at the path: to the entity itself and, for a
directory, to its entries, but not to anything inside its subdirectories.

A path that cannot be watched, such as one that does not exist, gives no events and no error.
Subscriptions to the same path with the same recursiveness share one watcher, and each event
goes to all of them.

values.name: watchRecursive
values.comment:
Creates a subscription like [watch](#watch), which also reports changes anywhere inside the
directory's subdirectories.

values.name: writeFile
values.comment:
Writes the bytes into the file at the path, creating the file if it does not exist and
replacing its contents if it does.

This is [writeFileWith](#writeFileWith) with [defaultWriteOptions](#defaultWriteOptions).

values.name: writeFileStream
values.comment:
Opens the file at the path and returns a stream whose bytes are written into it, where `mode`
says. Close the stream when you are done writing to it.

The file is opened before the task succeeds, so a file that cannot be opened fails this task with
an [Error](#Error). A failure of the file while writing arrives on the stream as `Stream.Failed`,
which [fromStreamFailure](#fromStreamFailure) reads back as an `Error`.

This is [writeFileStreamWith](#writeFileStreamWith) with
[defaultWriteOptions](#defaultWriteOptions).

values.name: writeFileStreamWith
values.comment:
Opens a stream into the file at the path, as [writeFileStream](#writeFileStream) does, with the
[WriteOptions](#WriteOptions) given.

With `sync`, closing the stream succeeds only once the data has been flushed to the storage
device, and a failed flush fails the close. A cancelled stream is not flushed.
values.type: FileSystem.WriteOptions -> FileSystem.WriteFileStreamMode -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (Stream.Writable Bytes.Bytes)

values.name: writeFileWith
values.comment:
Writes the bytes into the file at the path, as [writeFile](#writeFile) does, with the
[WriteOptions](#WriteOptions) given.

    FileSystem.writeFileWith { defaultWriteOptions | createNew = True, sync = True } bytes path

With either option on, the file is opened (emptying an existing one, or failing with
[FileExists](#ErrorKind) for `createNew`), written from the beginning, flushed for `sync`, and closed. If a step after the
open fails, closing the file is still attempted, and the first failure is the one reported.
values.type: FileSystem.WriteOptions -> Bytes.Bytes -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error Path.Path

name: FileSystem.Handle
comment:
A program sometimes needs to keep a file open: to read and write it at chosen offsets, or to
go on acting on the file it opened after that file's path has been renamed or replaced. This
module does that with a [Handle](#Handle), which stands for one open file. Most programs need only
[FileSystem](FileSystem), whose tasks, apart from the file streams, each open and close whatever
they need; [FileSystem.writeFileWith](FileSystem#writeFileWith) also covers durable and exclusive
writes.

A handle's type records what it may be used for. In `Handle readAccess writeAccess`, the reading
functions accept a handle only if the first parameter is [ReadAccess](#ReadAccess), and the
functions that change the file only if the second is [WriteAccess](#WriteAccess). The function
that opened the file decides both, [makeReadOnly](#makeReadOnly) and
[makeWriteOnly](#makeWriteOnly) give one of them up, and [close](#close) takes any handle. Each
task that changes the file succeeds with the handle it was given, so that calls on one file can be
chained.

Reads and writes say where in the file they act, as a byte offset from its start. Apart from
[writeFromOffset](#writeFromOffset) with a negative offset, nothing here reads or moves a current
position in the file. [read](#read) reads the whole file and [write](#write) writes at offset 0,
so two `write`s overwrite each other rather than appending. To read or write a file from start to
end in pieces, use [FileSystem.readFileStream](FileSystem#readFileStream) and
[FileSystem.writeFileStream](FileSystem#writeFileStream).

A handle stays open until [close](#close). An operation on it started after that fails with
[HandleClosed](FileSystem#ErrorKind), unless its file descriptor, the operating system's number for an open file, has
since been reused for a file opened by this module or by
[FileSystem.writeFileWith](FileSystem#writeFileWith) with an option on, and that file is still
open. The closed handle then acts on that file.

A task that fails, fails with a [FileSystem.Error](FileSystem#Error). When opening fails,
[errorPath](FileSystem#errorPath) is the path that was being opened; for every operation on a
handle it is [Path.empty](Path#empty). The path to open reaches the operating system as
[Path.toPosixString](Path#toPosixString) prints it.

On the native backend under Windows, opening a file fails with
[NotSupported](FileSystem#ErrorKind), so no handle can be obtained there.

unions.name: Handle
unions.comment:
An open file, together with what its holder may do with it.

A handle comes from [openForRead](#openForRead), [openForWrite](#openForWrite) or
[openForReadAndWrite](#openForReadAndWrite), or is a copy of one. Its first type parameter can be
[ReadAccess](#ReadAccess) only if the file was opened for reading, and its second
[WriteAccess](#WriteAccess) only if it was opened for writing; the open functions put `Never` where
an access is absent. The converse does not hold: `openForWrite ExpectExisting` opens the file for
reading too, and its handle still has no read access.

Holding a handle is all it takes to use it within its access, so pass one only to code that should
have that access.

Copies of a handle, including those [makeReadOnly](#makeReadOnly) and
[makeWriteOnly](#makeWriteOnly) return, are the same open file, and closing one closes them all.

unions.name: OpenForWriteBehaviour
unions.comment:
What opening a file for writing does with whatever is at the path already.

`EnsureEmpty` creates the file if nothing exists at the path, and empties the file if it exists.

`ExpectExisting` opens the file with its contents as they are, and fails if nothing exists at the
path. It opens the file for reading as well as writing, whichever function opens it, so the
program must be allowed to read the file too.

`ExpectNotExisting` creates the file, and fails with [FileExists](FileSystem#ErrorKind) if
anything already exists at the path. The operating system checks and creates in one step (`O_EXCL`), so of two programs creating
the same file at most one succeeds.

A file that opening creates gets the mode `666`, less the bits the process's umask removes.

unions.name: ReadAccess
unions.comment:
The marker, in a [Handle](#Handle)'s first type parameter, that the handle may be read.

It is used only as a type parameter; a program cannot make a value of it.

unions.name: WriteAccess
unions.comment:
The marker, in a [Handle](#Handle)'s second type parameter, that the handle may be used to
change the file.

It is used only as a type parameter; a program cannot make a value of it.

aliases.name: ReadWriteableHandle
aliases.comment:
A [Handle](#Handle) that may be both read and used to change the file, as
[openForReadAndWrite](#openForReadAndWrite) returns.
aliases.type: FileSystem.Handle.Handle FileSystem.Handle.ReadAccess FileSystem.Handle.WriteAccess

aliases.name: ReadableHandle
aliases.comment: A [Handle](#Handle) that may be read, whatever its write access.
aliases.type: FileSystem.Handle.Handle FileSystem.Handle.ReadAccess a

aliases.name: WriteableHandle
aliases.comment: A [Handle](#Handle) that may be used to change the file, whatever its read access.
aliases.type: FileSystem.Handle.Handle a FileSystem.Handle.WriteAccess

values.name: changeAccess
values.comment:
Sets the access permissions of the open file, for its owner, its group and everyone else.

Each list becomes one octal digit of the file mode, as in
[FileSystem.changeAccess](FileSystem#changeAccess), so
`{ owner = [ Read, Write ], group = [ Read ], others = [ Read ] }` sets the mode `644`. The mode
has no other bits, so the set-user-ID, set-group-ID and sticky bits are cleared.
values.type: { owner : List.List FileSystem.AccessPermission, group : List.List FileSystem.AccessPermission, others : List.List FileSystem.AccessPermission } -> FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a)

values.name: changeOwner
values.comment: Sets the user and group that own the open file, given as numeric ids.
values.type: { userID : Basics.Int, groupID : Basics.Int } -> FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a)

values.name: changeTimes
values.comment:
Sets the last access and last modification times of the open file.

The times are set in whole seconds, as for [FileSystem.changeTimes](FileSystem#changeTimes): each
is sent as its milliseconds divided by 1000 with `//`, which rounds down for times after 1970 and
toward zero for times before. On the JS backend `//` gives a 32-bit result, so a time from
2038-01-19T03:14:08Z on, or at or before 1901-12-13T20:45:51Z, is sent wrapped round into that
range, and a different time is set.
values.type: { lastAccessed : Time.Posix, lastModified : Time.Posix } -> FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a)

values.name: close
values.comment:
Closes the file.

The handle, and every copy of it, counts as closed from then on, even if closing fails. An
operation on it started afterwards, a second `close` included, fails with
[HandleClosed](FileSystem#ErrorKind), except after the reuse of its file descriptor that the
module documentation describes.

values.name: makeReadOnly
values.comment:
Returns the same open file as a handle that may only be read, for passing to code that should
not change the file. Closing either handle closes the file.

values.name: makeWriteOnly
values.comment:
Returns the same open file as a handle that may only be used to change the file, for passing
to code that should not read it. Closing either handle closes the file.

values.name: metadata
values.comment:
Returns the metadata of the open file, with the fields
[FileSystem.Metadata](FileSystem#Metadata) describes.

Its `entityType` is never `Symlink`: opening a path that names a symbolic link opens the entity
the link points to.

values.name: openForRead
values.comment:
Opens the file at the path for reading. The task fails if the file cannot be opened, as when
nothing exists at the path.

values.name: openForReadAndWrite
values.comment:
Opens the file at the path for both reading and writing, treating what is already there as the
[OpenForWriteBehaviour](#OpenForWriteBehaviour) says.

values.name: openForWrite
values.comment:
Opens the file at the path for writing, treating what is already there as the
[OpenForWriteBehaviour](#OpenForWriteBehaviour) says.
values.type: FileSystem.Handle.OpenForWriteBehaviour -> Path.Path -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (FileSystem.Handle.Handle Basics.Never FileSystem.Handle.WriteAccess)

values.name: read
values.comment: Reads the whole file, from its first byte to its end.

values.name: readFromOffset
values.comment:
Reads up to `length` bytes, starting `offset` bytes into the file.

Fewer bytes come back if the end of the file comes first, and none if `offset` is at or past it.
A negative `length` reads to the end of the file, and a negative `offset` reads from the start.
values.type: FileSystem.Handle.ReadableHandle a -> { offset : Basics.Int, length : Basics.Int } -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error Bytes.Bytes

values.name: sync
values.comment:
Flushes the file's changes, its data and its metadata, from the operating system's buffers to
the storage device (`fsync`), and succeeds once the operating system reports them written.

values.name: syncData
values.comment:
Flushes the file's data to the storage device, as [sync](#sync) does, but with `fdatasync`,
which may leave metadata that reading the data back does not need, such as the times, unwritten.

On the native backend under macOS it asks instead for `F_FULLFSYNC`, which also flushes the
storage device's own cache, and uses `fsync` if that fails; [sync](#sync) there uses `fsync`
alone.

values.name: truncate
values.comment:
Sets the size of the file to `length` bytes. A longer file loses the bytes past `length`, and a
shorter one is extended with zero bytes.

A negative `length` fails with [InvalidInput](FileSystem#ErrorKind) on the native backend, and empties the file on the JS
backend.
values.type: Basics.Int -> FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a)

values.name: write
values.comment:
Writes the bytes at the start of the file.

The bytes already in the file are overwritten where the new ones fall, and any past them are
kept: the file is not shortened. [writeFromOffset](#writeFromOffset) writes elsewhere, and
[truncate](#truncate) shortens the file.
values.type: FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a -> Bytes.Bytes -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a)

values.name: writeFromOffset
values.comment:
Writes the bytes into the file starting `offset` bytes from its start, overwriting what is
there.

A negative `offset` writes at the open file's current position instead. That position is the
start of the file when it is opened, and only a write with a negative offset moves it, to just
past the bytes written. So a sequence of such writes, each started after the one before has
succeeded, through any copies of the handle, puts its bytes one after another.
values.type: FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a -> Basics.Int -> Bytes.Bytes -> Task.Task FileSystem.Error (FileSystem.Handle.WriteableHandle a)

name: Html.Dom
comment:
`Html` is opaque in elm/html, so a program can build a page but can neither look inside it nor turn it into text. This module gives every `Html` and `Svg` value (a `VirtualDom.Node`) a transparent view, [`Node`](#Node), and serializes it to HTML text. [`fromHtml`](#fromHtml) turns any `Html msg` into a `Node` you can pattern-match on, and [`fromAttribute`](#fromAttribute) turns an `Html.Attribute msg` into a [`Fact`](#Fact): one attribute, namespaced attribute, property, style or event handler of an element. [`toString`](#toString) serializes a `Node`, [`htmlToString`](#htmlToString) serializes `Html`, and [`attributes`](#attributes) gives the attributes an element's opening tag gets. import Html exposing (div, text) import Html.Attributes exposing (class) import Html.Dom Html.Dom.htmlToString (div [ class "greeting" ] [ text "Hello & welcome" ]) --> "
Hello & welcome
" **One serialization, two implementations.** `toString` is written in Elm, over a `Node`; `htmlToString` is the kernel's, over `Html`, and the two produce the same text. On the native target an `Html` value already is a `Node`, so `fromHtml` and `fromAttribute` cost nothing and `htmlToString` is a C++ copy of `toString`'s rules. On the JavaScript target `fromHtml` copies the tree into a `Node` and `htmlToString` is `toString` applied to that copy. On the JavaScript target the order of an element's attributes may differ from the native target, and so may the `class` joined from several `className` properties when one of their values is not a string. **Which attributes are written.** The facts of an element are combined before they are written: - Attributes, namespaced attributes and styles are each applied as one group, at the position of the first fact of their kind; each property is applied at the position of its first occurrence. Between two facts of one kind with the same name, the later wins, except that `class` attributes are joined with a space, and so are `className` properties. - On an HTML element (one with no namespace) the names of attributes, but not of namespaced attributes, are lower-cased. A namespaced attribute is written under its name alone; its namespace is not written. - A property that has a matching attribute is written as that attribute: `className` as `class`, `htmlFor` as `for`, `id`, `href`, `title` and the like under their own names. Every property that an `Html.Attributes` function other than `property` and `value` makes is one of these. A boolean property such as `checked` or `disabled` is written as a bare attribute when its value is true in JavaScript's sense, and removes the attribute otherwise; `contentEditable` and `spellcheck` are exceptions, written with their value as text. `value` is the content of an HTML `textarea`, is not written on a `select` or on a namespaced `textarea`, and is the `value` attribute on other elements. Any other property, such as `innerHTML`, is not written. - Styles are written as declarations in the `style` attribute. A camel-case name is written in CSS form (`backgroundColor` as `background-color`), and an empty value removes the declaration. A `style` attribute applied after styles replaces them. - Event handlers are never written. **How text is written.** Text is escaped (`&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'`), and so are attribute values (`&`, `"`, `<` and `>`). The one exception is the text of an HTML `style` element, which is written as it is except that ``, `/`, or, in an attribute name, `=`. An attribute with such a name is dropped, and an element with such a tag is replaced by its children. Neither `toString` nor `htmlToString` writes ``; [`Http.Server.setBodyAsHtml`](Http-Server#setBodyAsHtml) adds one when the root element is `html`. **What is not modelled.** A string-valued property whose value is an array or an object is not written. Text inside `script`, `xmp`, `iframe`, `noembed`, `noframes` and `noscript` is escaped like any other text. **Laziness.** An `Html.Lazy` subtree is always computed: natively when the node is built, on the JavaScript target each time `fromHtml` or `htmlToString` reaches it. **Equality.** `==` on a `Node` that contains a `Mapped` node or an `Event` fact compares the functions and decoders inside them, so it has the same restriction as `==` on `Html`. @docs Node, Fact, Tagger, Handler # Converting @docs fromHtml, fromAttribute # Rendering @docs attributes, toString, htmlToString

unions.name: Fact
unions.comment:
One fact of an element: an `Html.Attribute`, as data.

`Attribute` carries a name and a value.

`AttributeNS` carries the namespace, then the name and the value.

`Property` sets a DOM property to a JSON value. Many `Html.Attributes` functions make
properties rather than attributes: `Html.Attributes.class` is `Property "className"`, and
`Html.Attributes.checked` is `Property "checked"`.

`Style` carries a CSS property name, as given to `Html.Attributes.style`, and its value.

`Event` carries the event name, the [`Handler`](#Handler) and a list of
[`Tagger`](#Tagger)s. Natively the list holds the functions given to `Html.Attributes.map`,
outermost first; on the JavaScript target it is always empty, because elm/virtual-dom folds
those functions into the handler. A `Handler` can only come from `fromHtml` or
`fromAttribute`, so a program can build an `Event` fact only with a `Handler` taken from one of
those.

unions.name: Handler
unions.comment:
An event handler: a `VirtualDom.Handler`, which holds the decoder for the event and says
how its message is handled.

A value can only be obtained from [`fromHtml`](#fromHtml) or [`fromAttribute`](#fromAttribute),
and nothing in this module uses one.

unions.name: Node
unions.comment:
A node of an `Html` or `Svg` tree, as data.

`Text` is a text node. Its string is escaped when serialized, except inside an HTML `style`
element.

`Element` carries the namespace, the tag, the facts and the children. The namespace is
`Nothing` for an HTML element and `Just` the namespace given to `VirtualDom.nodeNS` otherwise
(the SVG namespace for an `Svg` node).

`KeyedElement` is a keyed element, such as one made with `Html.Keyed`, laid out like `Element`
except that each child is paired with its key. The keys are not serialized.

`Mapped` is a node made with `Html.map`: it keeps the function, and the node it wraps is the one
serialized.

A [`Tagger`](#Tagger) can only come from `fromHtml` or `fromAttribute`, so a program can build
`Text`, `Element` and `KeyedElement` nodes from scratch, but a `Mapped` node only around a
`Tagger` taken from one of those.

unions.name: Tagger
unions.comment:
A function given to `Html.map` or `Html.Attributes.map`, as kept in a `Mapped` node or an
`Event` fact.

A value can only be obtained from [`fromHtml`](#fromHtml) or [`fromAttribute`](#fromAttribute),
and nothing in this module applies one.

values.name: attributes
values.comment:
Returns the attributes `toString` writes in an element's opening tag, in order and with
their values unescaped, after the facts have been combined as the module documentation
describes. `Nothing` is a bare attribute, such as `checked`. A `Mapped` node gives the
attributes of the node it wraps, and a `Text` node gives none.

For an element whose tag is token-breaking, which `toString` replaces by its children, this
still returns the attributes the element would have had.

values.name: fromAttribute
values.comment: Returns the `Fact` view of any `Html.Attribute msg`.

values.name: fromHtml
values.comment:
Returns the `Node` view of any `Html msg` or `Svg msg`.

On the native target this costs nothing, because an `Html` value already is a `Node`. On the
JavaScript target the tree is copied, computing every `Html.Lazy` subtree. Each element's facts
arrive already combined by elm/virtual-dom, where natively they are the list as given. On the
JavaScript target a node made by a kernel's custom renderer becomes an empty `div` with that
node's facts.

values.name: htmlToString
values.comment:
Returns the HTML text of an `Html` or `Svg` value: the same text as `toString (fromHtml html)`.

The result has no `<!DOCTYPE html>`. Add one yourself for a whole document, or use
[`Http.Server.setBodyAsHtml`](Http-Server#setBodyAsHtml), which adds it when the root element
is `html`.

values.name: toString
values.comment:
Returns the HTML text of a `Node`, by the rules in the module documentation. For a
`Node` made by `fromHtml html` it produces the same text as [`htmlToString`](#htmlToString)
`html`.

name: Http.Method
comment:
The method of an HTTP request, shared by the server and the client side of this package.

[`Http.Server`](Http-Server) gives the method of every request it receives as a
[`Method`](#Method), and [`Http.Stream`](Http-Stream) takes one for every request it sends.
The type has a module of its own so that a program that only sends requests need not import the
server module to name a method. The rest of what an HTTP client needs, such as `Http.Header` and
`Http.Error`, comes from [elm/http](/packages/elm/http/latest/).

    import Http.Method exposing (Method(..))

    Http.Method.toString OPTIONS
    --> "OPTIONS"

@docs Method, toString, fromString

unions.name: Method
unions.comment:
An HTTP method.

The constructors are the methods of RFC 9110 and `PATCH` (RFC 5789), spelled as they are sent.
`UNKNOWN` holds the name of any other method, as it was received or is to be sent, for example
`UNKNOWN "PROPFIND"`.

values.name: fromString
values.comment:
Returns the method named `name`.

Method names are case-sensitive in HTTP, so the name is matched exactly: `"GET"` gives `GET`,
while `"get"` gives `UNKNOWN "get"`. Any name that is not one of the constructors gives
`UNKNOWN name`, so `fromString` and [`toString`](#toString) give back the name they were given.

    Http.Method.fromString "OPTIONS"
    --> OPTIONS

    Http.Method.fromString "get"
    --> UNKNOWN "get"

values.name: toString
values.comment:
Returns the name of a method, for example `"GET"`. `UNKNOWN name` gives `name`.

    Http.Method.toString PATCH
    --> "PATCH"

    Http.Method.toString (UNKNOWN "PROPFIND")
    --> "PROPFIND"

name: Http.Server
comment:
An HTTP server for an Elm program: requests arrive as subscription messages, and the program
answers each one by sending a response as a command.

[`listen`](#listen) or [`listenOnHost`](#listenOnHost) starts a [`Server`](#Server).
[`onRequest`](#onRequest) subscribes to its requests, and every [`Request`](#Request) arrives
together with a fresh [`Response`](#Response), which the program builds up and
[`send`](#send)s from its `update` function:

    GotRequest request response ->
        ( model
        , response
            |> Http.Server.setHeader "Content-Type" "text/html"
            |> Http.Server.setBody "<html>Hello there!</html>"
            |> Http.Server.send
        )

A response answers the one request it arrived with. It carries that request's _response key_,
the server's name for a request that is still waiting for its answer. The key is released when
the request is answered, when [`upgradeRequest`](#upgradeRequest) takes the request over, and
when the request's connection goes away. From then on, sending the response writes nothing, so a
request is answered at most once however often its response is sent.

The server speaks HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 over TLS, or both, as its `protocols` say (see
[`ListenOptions`](#ListenOptions)). Over HTTP/1 a connection is kept alive and serves one request
after another; requests a client sends ahead of their answers (pipelining) are handed to the
program one at a time, in order, each once the one before it has been answered. Over HTTP/2
several requests on one connection are handed over at once and answered independently.

The server checks every request against its limits and the HTTP rules before the program sees
it. A request that breaks them never arrives: the server answers it itself, with a status such
as 400, 413 or 431, or over HTTP/2 may reset its stream instead.

Starting a server fails with this module's own [`Error`](#Error). On the native backend under
Windows no server can be started (`listen` and `listenOnHost` fail with
[`NotSupported`](#ErrorKind)), and an `onRequest` subscription stops the program with a fatal
error.


## Servers

@docs Server, ListenOptions, defaultListenOptions, listen, listenOnHost, endpoint, close, closeWithin


## Requests

@docs Request, HttpVersion, Upgrade, bodyAsString, bodyAsJson, requestToString, onRequest


## Responses

A fresh response has status `200`, no headers and an empty body.

@docs Response, send

@docs setStatus, setHeader, appendHeader


### Body

@docs setBody, setBodyAsString, setBodyAsBytes, setBodyAsHtml


## WebSockets

## Errors
