unions.name: Error
unions.comment:
A failure to start a server, from [`listen`](#listen) or [`listenOnHost`](#listenOnHost).

[`errorKind`](#errorKind) says what kind of failure it is, and [`errorToString`](#errorToString)
describes it for people to read.

This is a separate type from `Socket.Error`, and from the [`WebSocket.Error`](WebSocket#Error)
that [`upgradeRequest`](#upgradeRequest) fails with, so that a server program matches only on what
starting a server can produce.

unions.name: ErrorKind
unions.comment:
What kind of failure an [`Error`](#Error) is.

  - `AddressInUse` (`EADDRINUSE`): the port is already in use, for example by another server.
  - `AddressNotAvailable` (`EADDRNOTAVAIL`, `EAFNOSUPPORT`): the address does not belong to this
    machine, or the system does not support its family.
  - `HostNotFound` (`ENOTFOUND`, `EAI_FAIL`): the host name given to
    [`listenOnHost`](#listenOnHost) has no address.
  - `HostLookupTryAgain` (`EAI_AGAIN`): the resolver could not answer for now; trying again later
    may succeed.
  - `PermissionDenied` (`EACCES`, `EPERM`): the operating system refused to listen, for example
    on a privileged port.
  - `InvalidPort` (`ERR_SOCKET_BAD_PORT`): the port is outside 0 to 65535.
  - `InvalidInput` (`EINVAL`): the options cannot be used, as empty `protocols` or `Http2` without `tls`.
  - `NotSupported` (`ENOTSUP`): no server can be started here, as on the native backend under
    Windows.
  - `CertificateUnusable reason`: the TLS certificate chain or private key cannot be used, for
    example because it is not PEM or the key does not belong to the certificate. `reason` is the
    TLS library's reason, upper-cased with underscores, such as `"NO_CERTIFICATES"`. This is not
    [`Socket.Tls.CertificateRejected`](Socket-Tls#Problem), which is a peer's certificate failing
    verification.
  - `OtherServerError code`: any other failure, with the code the system reported, such as an
    errno name.

unions.name: HttpVersion
unions.comment:
The HTTP version a request was made with, or one a server offers in the `protocols` of its
[`ListenOptions`](#ListenOptions). A request is made with `Http2` only on a server whose `protocols`
include it.

unions.name: Server
unions.comment:
An HTTP server that [`listen`](#listen) or [`listenOnHost`](#listenOnHost) started.

A `Server` stays usable after it has been closed: [`endpoint`](#endpoint) still answers, and
closing it again does nothing.

unions.name: Upgrade
unions.comment:
The protocol a request asks to switch to, from its `upgrade` field.

`WebSocketUpgrade` is a WebSocket opening request (`websocket`), to be taken over with
[`upgradeRequest`](#upgradeRequest). `UnknownUpgrade` holds any other protocol, lower-cased, as
it was received, for example `UnknownUpgrade "h2c"`. The server switches to no other protocol
itself, so the program answers such a request with a normal response, which refuses the upgrade.

The protocol name is compared after lower-casing, so `Upgrade: WebSocket` is a
`WebSocketUpgrade` too.

aliases.name: ListenOptions
aliases.comment:
How to run a server: where it listens, whether it uses TLS and HTTP/2, and the limits it holds
clients to.

`port_` 0 lets the system pick a free port, which [`endpoint`](#endpoint) reports.

`tls` serves HTTPS (and so `wss` WebSockets) with the given certificate chain and key. Its `alpn`
field is not used: the server offers its `protocols` instead, `h2` for HTTP/2 and `http/1.1`
for HTTP/1.

`protocols` are the [HTTP versions](#HttpVersion) the server serves, as a set: their order does
not matter, repeats are ignored, and a client that can use both HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 is served
HTTP/2. `Http1_0` and `Http1_1` both serve HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1. `Http2` serves HTTP/2 to
clients that choose it during the TLS handshake, so it requires `tls`, and TLS 1.2 is then limited
to the cipher suites HTTP/2 allows. With HTTP/1, a TLS client that offers neither name, or none at
all, is still served HTTP/1.1; without it, such a client is refused. `protocols` must not be empty.

`maxConnections` is the most connections open at once. Natively, further clients wait in the
operating system's queue of pending connections until one closes; on the JavaScript backend Node
drops them.

`maxConcurrentStreams` is the most HTTP/2 requests, WebSockets included, in progress at once on one
connection, and is advertised to the client. Natively, requests the program has not answered yet
count even when the client has cancelled them, and at the limit the server processes nothing more
from that connection until the program answers one; on the JavaScript backend Node refuses the
requests over the limit. Without this limit, natively a client that keeps cancelling its requests
is held back only by a limit on cancellations (about 1000 at once, then 33 per second), so a
public server should set one.

For both of these limits `Nothing` means no limit, but `Just 0` or a negative value is a limit of
0, which serves nothing. A `maxConnections` of 0 natively accepts no connection, so clients wait
indefinitely, and on the JavaScript backend drops every one. A `maxConcurrentStreams` of 0 refuses
every HTTP/2 request.

`maxBodySize` and `maxHeaderSize` are in bytes. A request with a larger body is answered 413, and
one with a larger header block 431 (on the JavaScript backend over HTTP/2, a header block over
twice `maxHeaderSize` has its stream reset instead).

`keepAliveTimeout`, `headersTimeout` and `requestTimeout` are in milliseconds, and a value of 0 or
less is no timeout. `keepAliveTimeout` is how long an idle connection stays open between requests.
`headersTimeout` runs from the first byte of a request to the end of its headers and
`requestTimeout` to the end of its body; a request that takes longer is answered 408. Natively, a
new connection without TLS that sends nothing is closed after `headersTimeout`. Over HTTP/2 they
apply differently: natively `headersTimeout` limits only the wait for a new connection's first
bytes, and on the JavaScript backend none of the three applies. No timeout limits the program's
answer: the connection waits for it.
aliases.type: { address : Socket.Address.Address, port_ : Basics.Int, tls : Maybe.Maybe Socket.Tls.ServerOptions, protocols : List.List Http.Server.HttpVersion, maxConnections : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int, maxConcurrentStreams : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int, maxBodySize : Basics.Int, maxHeaderSize : Basics.Int, keepAliveTimeout : Basics.Int, headersTimeout : Basics.Int, requestTimeout : Basics.Int }

aliases.name: Request
aliases.comment:
An HTTP request a server has received.

`headers` maps each header name, spelled as the client sent it, to its value. Over HTTP/2 names
are always lower case, and over HTTP/1 they need not be, so look a header up by every spelling it
may have or compare names case-insensitively: names that differ in case are separate entries. When
a name is sent more than once with the same spelling, the last value wins. Over HTTP/2 the
pseudo-header fields (`:method`, `:path`, ...) are not included, and several `cookie` fields are
joined into one with `"; "`.

`body` is the complete request body.

`url` is the absolute URL of the request, made from the `Host` header (over HTTP/2 the
`:authority` field), or, without one, the host the server was started with (its address for
`listen`, `localhost` for `listenOnHost ""`) and its port, followed by the request target; a target
that is already an absolute URL is used as it is. When that text is not one `Url.fromString`
accepts, for example when the host is a bracketed IPv6 address, `url` has an empty host and path,
and its protocol is `Https` when the connection uses TLS and `Http` otherwise.

`method` is the request's [`Http.Method.Method`](Http-Method#Method), for example `GET`; a method
that has no constructor of its own is `UNKNOWN` with its name as received, such as
`UNKNOWN "PROPFIND"`.

`upgrade` is the protocol the client asks to switch to, as an [`Upgrade`](#Upgrade), such as
`Just WebSocketUpgrade`: the first protocol of the HTTP/1.1 `Upgrade` header when `Connection`
also names `upgrade` (natively, only for a request without a body), or HTTP/2's `:protocol`.
Answer a WebSocket request with [`upgradeRequest`](#upgradeRequest). Any response sent instead
refuses the upgrade, and over HTTP/1 the connection then closes.
aliases.type: { headers : Dict.Dict String.String String.String, method : Http.Method.Method, body : Bytes.Bytes, url : Url.Url, version : Http.Server.HttpVersion, upgrade : Maybe.Maybe Http.Server.Upgrade }

aliases.name: Response
aliases.comment:
An HTTP response being built for one request.

A response is obtained only from [`onRequest`](#onRequest), together with the request it answers,
and stays tied to that request: the functions below change its status, headers and body, but
never which request it answers.
aliases.type: Http.Server.Internal.Response

values.name: appendHeader
values.comment:
Adds a value to the header with exactly this name, after the values it already has, or adds
the header last. Use this for headers that may appear more than once, such as `Set-Cookie`.

values.name: bodyAsJson
values.comment:
Decodes the request body as JSON. A body that is not valid UTF-8 is decoded as the empty
string, so the decoder fails.
values.type: Json.Decode.Decoder a -> Http.Server.Request -> Result.Result Json.Decode.Error a

values.name: bodyAsString
values.comment: Returns the request body as a string, or `Nothing` if it is not valid UTF-8.

values.name: close
values.comment: Stops a server gracefully, with [`closeWithin`](#closeWithin) and a deadline of 5 seconds.

values.name: closeWithin
values.comment:
Stops a server gracefully, closing the connections still open after `deadline` milliseconds.

The server stops accepting connections at once (the port is free when the task completes) and
closes its idle connections. Requests held because nothing subscribed to them (see
[`onRequest`](#onRequest)) are answered 503. Requests already handed to the program can still be
answered until the deadline, over HTTP/1 with `Connection: close`; then the connections that remain
are closed. A request still being received when the server closes can still be handed to a
subscription. WebSockets made with [`upgradeRequest`](#upgradeRequest) stay open, except one over
HTTP/2, which shares its connection and ends with it at the deadline.

Closing a server twice is fine. Once the deadline has passed, nothing of a closed server keeps the program
running.

values.name: defaultListenOptions
values.comment:
Returns the options for plain HTTP/1.1 on `address` and `port_`, with no connection or stream
limits, bodies up to 16 MiB, header blocks up to 64 KiB, a 5 second keep-alive timeout, a 60
second headers timeout and a 300 second request timeout.

    Http.Server.defaultListenOptions (Socket.Address.loopback Socket.Address.IPv4) 8080

values.name: endpoint
values.comment:
Returns the address and port a server listens on. For port 0 this is the port the system
picked. An address the system reports as text that does not parse is given as `0.0.0.0`.

values.name: errorKind
values.comment:
Returns what kind of failure the error is.

    case Http.Server.errorKind error of
        Http.Server.AddressInUse ->
            "the port is taken"

        _ ->
            Http.Server.errorToString error

values.name: errorToString
values.comment:
Returns a human readable description of the error: the code the system reported, `": "`, and
the message, as in `"EADDRINUSE: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:8080"`.

values.name: listen
values.comment:
Starts a server as `options` say.

    let
        options =
            Http.Server.defaultListenOptions (Socket.Address.loopback Socket.Address.IPv4) 8443
    in
    Http.Server.listen
        { options | tls = Just { certificateChain = cert, privateKey = key, alpn = [] } }

Fails with an [`Error`](#Error): for example of kind [`AddressInUse`](#ErrorKind) when the port
is taken, [`CertificateUnusable`](#ErrorKind) when the certificate chain or key cannot be used,
[`InvalidPort`](#ErrorKind) for a port outside 0 to 65535, and [`InvalidInput`](#ErrorKind) when
`protocols` is empty or has `Http2` without `tls`. A listening server keeps the program running only while an [`onRequest`](#onRequest) subscription to it exists or
a request it handed over has not been answered.

values.name: listenOnHost
values.comment:
Starts a server listening on `host` and `port_`, with the limits and timeouts of
[`defaultListenOptions`](#defaultListenOptions), and without TLS.

    Http.Server.listenOnHost "localhost" 8080

An address literal such as `"127.0.0.1"` or `"::1"` is used as it is. A name is resolved, and the
server listens on one of its addresses; natively that is the first IPv4 address that can be used,
if there is one. The empty string listens on every interface: natively on `0.0.0.0`, so on IPv4
only, and on the JavaScript backend on Node's default, `::` where IPv6 is available. Port 0 lets
the system pick a free port, which [`endpoint`](#endpoint) reports.

A name that cannot be resolved fails with kind [`HostNotFound`](#ErrorKind), or
[`HostLookupTryAgain`](#ErrorKind) when the resolver could not answer for now. A
listening server keeps the program running only while an [`onRequest`](#onRequest) subscription to
it exists or a request it handed over has not been answered.

values.name: onRequest
values.comment:
Creates a subscription to the requests `server` receives, each with a fresh
[`Response`](#Response) that answers it.

    subscriptions : Model -> Sub Msg
    subscriptions model =
        Http.Server.onRequest model.server GotRequest

Every subscription to one server receives every request, all with the same response, so only the
first of them to be sent answers it.

Requests that arrive while nothing subscribes to their server are held, and handed out oldest
first once a subscription appears. A server holds about `maxBodySize` × 4 bytes of them, and
always at least one. It answers 503 to a request beyond that, and to a request that arrives
after the server was closed with nothing subscribed.

values.name: requestToString
values.comment:
Returns a one-line description of a request for logs: its method and URL, for example
`"GET http://localhost:8080/"`. An `UNKNOWN` method is written as `UNKNOWN(name)`, so that it
cannot be mistaken for one of the methods that have a constructor.

values.name: send
values.comment:
Creates a command that sends `response` to the request it answers.

The response is written with its status, its headers in order, one header line per value, and
its body:

  - A `Content-Length` header is always written, except with status 204 or 304, which send no
    body. The response's own `Content-Length`, `Connection` and `Transfer-Encoding` headers are
    left out, and so is a header whose name is empty or whose name or value holds a carriage
    return, line feed or NUL character. On the JavaScript backend a header Node considers invalid,
    such as one whose name contains a space, is left out as well. A `Date` header is added unless
    the response has one.
  - Over HTTP/2 header names are sent lower-cased, and other headers HTTP/2 forbids, such as
    `Upgrade` and `Keep-Alive`, are left out too. On the JavaScript backend, if a header HTTP/2
    allows only once, such as `Content-Type`, has several values (for example from two spellings
    of its name), every header of the response that has several values keeps only its last one.
  - The answer to a `HEAD` request has the headers only.
  - An HTML body (see [`setBodyAsHtml`](#setBodyAsHtml)) is serialized now.

Over HTTP/1 the connection then stays open for the client's next request, unless, for example,
the client asked to close it (`Connection: close`, or HTTP/1.0 without keep-alive), the response
has a `Connection: close` header, the server is closing, or the request asked to switch protocols
or was a `CONNECT`.

Sending a response whose request was already answered, was taken over by
[`upgradeRequest`](#upgradeRequest), or lost its connection writes nothing.

values.name: setBody
values.comment: Sets the body of a response to a string; the same as [`setBodyAsString`](#setBodyAsString).

values.name: setBodyAsBytes
values.comment: Sets the body of a response to bytes, which are sent as they are.

values.name: setBodyAsHtml
values.comment:
Sets the body of a response to an HTML page or fragment built with
[elm/html](/packages/elm/html/latest/) (or `Svg`).

    response
        |> Http.Server.setBodyAsHtml
            (Html.node "html" [] [ Html.node "body" [] [ Html.text "Hello!" ] ])
        |> Http.Server.send

When the response is sent:

  - the HTML is written as the text [`Html.Dom.htmlToString`](Html-Dom#htmlToString) gives,
    encoded as UTF-8, with the same lone-surrogate difference between the backends as
    [`setBodyAsString`](#setBodyAsString);
  - `<!DOCTYPE html>` is written first when the root, seen through `Html.map`, is an HTML `html`
    element;
  - `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8` is added unless the response already has a
    `Content-Type` header, in any case.

values.name: setBodyAsString
values.comment:
Sets the body of a response to a string, which is sent encoded as UTF-8. The backends differ
only for a lone surrogate: the JavaScript backend sends it as U+FFFD, the native one in its 3-byte
form, which is not valid UTF-8.

values.name: setHeader
values.comment:
Sets a header on a response, replacing the values of the header with exactly this name and
keeping its place, or adding it last. Names are compared exactly, so `"content-type"` does not
replace `"Content-Type"`: the response then has both.

values.name: setStatus
values.comment:
Sets the HTTP status code of a response. A status below 200 or above 999 is sent as 500.

    response |> Http.Server.setStatus 404

values.name: upgradeRequest
values.comment:
Takes over a WebSocket opening request (a [`Request`](#Request) whose `upgrade` is
`Just WebSocketUpgrade`, over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2) instead of answering it with its
[`Response`](#Response). The result is a [`WebSocket.Upgrade`](WebSocket#Upgrade), to be answered
with [`WebSocket.accept`](WebSocket#accept) or [`WebSocket.reject`](WebSocket#reject). The response
is used up: sending it later writes nothing.

    GotRequest request response ->
        if request.upgrade == Just Http.Server.WebSocketUpgrade then
            ( model
            , Http.Server.upgradeRequest request response
                |> Task.andThen (WebSocket.accept WebSocket.defaultAcceptOptions)
                |> Task.attempt GotWebSocket
            )

        else
            ...

The opening request is checked by `WebSocket.accept`, which answers a request that breaks the
rules with 400 or 426 itself, as for [`WebSocket.receiveUpgrade`](WebSocket#receiveUpgrade). Over
HTTP/1.1 the requests the client sent before this one on the same connection are answered first,
so the `101` follows their responses.

Over HTTP/2 the request is an extended `CONNECT` with `:protocol` `websocket`, which a server with
`Http2` allows; the server itself answers any other `:protocol` with 501. The WebSocket then runs
on that one stream of the connection, next to the connection's other requests and WebSockets:
`accept` answers `200` and the stream carries the frames, the close handshake ends the stream, and
an aborted WebSocket resets it. Such a WebSocket is one of the connection's streams for
`maxConcurrentStreams`.

The WebSocket does not belong to the server: [`close`](#close) leaves it open, except that over
HTTP/2 it ends at the close deadline with the connection it shares.

Fails with a [`WebSocket.Error`](WebSocket#Error): with `SocketError` of kind
[`Socket.InvalidInput`](Socket#ErrorKind) when the request does not ask for a WebSocket, in which
case the response is untouched and can still be sent; of kind `Socket.InvalidInput` too when the
request was already answered or taken over; and of kind `Socket.InvalidInput` or
[`Socket.Cancelled`](Socket#ErrorKind) when its connection has gone away.

The program keeps running until the `Upgrade` has been accepted or rejected with
`WebSocket.accept` or `WebSocket.reject`, or its connection has gone away.

name: Http.Stream
comment:
Lets a program send HTTP requests whose bodies are streams, so that it can upload or
download something large, or something that arrives slowly, without holding all of it in
memory.

This module extends [`elm/http`](/packages/elm/http/latest). A request body can be a
[`Stream.Readable`](Stream#Readable) of bytes, sent as it is read, and a response body can be
handed to the program as a `Stream.Readable Bytes`, to be read chunk by chunk while it
downloads. Everything that is not about streams stays elm/http's: headers are made with
`Http.header`, and results are elm/http's `Http.Error`, `Http.Metadata` and `Http.Response`.
This module has its own [`Body`](#Body), [`Expect`](#Expect) and [`Resolver`](#Resolver)
types, and its own [`request`](#request) and [`task`](#task), shaped like elm/http's. The method
of a request is an [`Http.Method.Method`](Http-Method#Method) rather than elm/http's `String`.

A request has two stages, and a failure is reported differently in each. Until the headers of
the final response arrive, the request itself can fail, with `Http.BadUrl`, `Http.Timeout` or
`Http.NetworkError`. Once they have arrived the response is handed over. A failure after that
point, such as the connection closing before the body is complete, reaches the body stream
instead: once the bytes already received have been read, a read of the body fails with
`Stream.Failed`, which [`fromStreamFailure`](#fromStreamFailure) reads as `Http.NetworkError`.

Differences from elm/http:

  - A URL with a scheme other than `http:` or `https:` fails with `Http.BadUrl`. A URL with no
    scheme fails with `Http.BadUrl` on the JavaScript backend.
  - The `timeout` covers everything up to the arrival of the final response's headers,
    including connecting, following redirects and sending the body. Once the headers have
    arrived the body may take as long as it needs.
  - There is no `tracker`, so `Http.track` and `Http.cancel` do not apply. To cancel a request,
    run it with [`task`](#task) in a process started with `Process.spawn`, and stop it with
    `Process.kill` before the response headers arrive. After that, cancel the body stream
    with `Stream.cancelReadable`, which stops a transfer still running. While a read is
    waiting on the body stream, or a pipe is reading it, `cancelReadable` fails with `Locked`
    and does nothing.
  - Redirects are followed, at most 20 of them; one more fails with `Http.NetworkError`, and a
    redirect to a URL that is not `http:` or `https:` fails with `Http.BadUrl` carrying the URL
    of the request. The status, headers and `Metadata.url` are those of the final response.

Response header names are lower-cased, and a header that appears more than once has its values
joined with `", "` in the order they arrived, as elm/http joins them.

unions.name: Body
unions.comment:
The body of a request made with this module: nothing, a block of bytes, or a stream.

A body other than [`emptyBody`](#emptyBody) carries a MIME type, and a non-empty MIME type is
sent as the `Content-Type` header, unless it holds a CR or LF (or, on the JavaScript backend,
something else Node rejects in a header value). An empty MIME type adds no `Content-Type` header
on the JavaScript backend; on the native backend libcurl can add
`Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` in its place. A body is made with
[`emptyBody`](#emptyBody), [`stringBody`](#stringBody), [`jsonBody`](#jsonBody),
[`bytesBody`](#bytesBody) or [`streamBody`](#streamBody).

unions.name: Expect
unions.comment:
How a [`request`](#request) turns its response into a message, as elm/http's `Http.Expect`
does. One is made with [`expectStream`](#expectStream), which keeps only a successful response's
body, or [`expectStreamResponse`](#expectStreamResponse), which keeps the body of every response.

unions.name: Resolver
unions.comment:
How a [`task`](#task) turns its response into the task's result: success with an `a`, or
failure with an `x`. One is made with [`streamResolver`](#streamResolver).

values.name: bytesBody
values.comment:
Makes a body holding `bytes`, sent with the
[MIME type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_type) `mimeType` as its `Content-Type` (an empty
`mimeType` is treated as [`Body`](#Body) describes). For example, to send an `archive.zip` file
made with [`elm/bytes`](/packages/elm/bytes/latest):

    zipBody : Bytes -> Http.Stream.Body
    zipBody bytes =
        Http.Stream.bytesBody "application/zip" bytes

values.name: emptyBody
values.comment:
A body with nothing in it, and no MIME type, so it adds no `Content-Type` header of its own.
On the native backend libcurl can still add `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
to a `POST`.

values.name: expectStream
values.comment:
Makes an [`Expect`](#Expect) that gives `toMsg` the response's metadata and its body
stream when the status code is in 200–299.

A status code outside 200–299 gives `Err (Http.BadStatus code)`, and the body is not downloaded:
the transfer is stopped as soon as the headers have arrived. A request that fails before the
headers arrive gives `Http.BadUrl`, `Http.Timeout` or `Http.NetworkError`.

Read the body to the end, or cancel it with `Stream.cancelReadable` once it is no longer needed.
Only about 256 KiB of unread body is held, so a larger body left unread keeps the transfer open.
values.type: (Result.Result Http.Error ( Http.Metadata, Stream.Readable Bytes.Bytes ) -> msg) -> Http.Stream.Expect msg

values.name: expectStreamResponse
values.comment:
Makes an [`Expect`](#Expect) that turns the whole `Http.Response` into a result with
`toResult` and gives that to `toMsg`, as elm/http's `Http.expectBytesResponse` does.

Unlike [`expectStream`](#expectStream), a response of any status code comes with its body
stream, so the body of, say, a 404 response can be read.
values.type: (Result.Result x a -> msg) -> (Http.Response (Stream.Readable Bytes.Bytes) -> Result.Result x a) -> Http.Stream.Expect msg

values.name: fromStreamFailure
values.comment:
Reads a failure of a response body stream as elm/http's `Http.Error`. Returns `Nothing` for a
failure that another module's stream made.

    case streamError of
        Stream.Failed failure ->
            case Http.Stream.fromStreamFailure failure of
                Just Http.NetworkError ->
                    "the download was cut off"

                _ ->
                    Stream.failureToString failure

        _ ->
            ...

Every failure of a body stream is `Http.NetworkError`: the connection closing before the body is
complete, the transfer failing, or a [`streamBody`](#streamBody) whose stream failed. Once the
response headers have arrived, the request no longer has a timeout, so a body stream never fails
with `Http.Timeout`. `Stream.failureToString` gives the details, such as the message the network
library reported.

values.name: jsonBody
values.comment:
Makes a body holding `value` as JSON text with no whitespace, sent with
`Content-Type: application/json`.

values.name: request
values.comment:
Sends a request and turns its response into a message, as `expect` says. For example, to
download a large file:

    import Bytes exposing (Bytes)
    import Http
    import Http.Method exposing (Method(..))
    import Http.Stream
    import Stream

    type Msg
        = GotStream (Result Http.Error ( Http.Metadata, Stream.Readable Bytes ))

    download : Cmd Msg
    download =
        Http.Stream.request
            { method = GET
            , headers = []
            , url = "https://example.com/large-file.csv"
            , body = Http.Stream.emptyBody
            , expect = Http.Stream.expectStream GotStream
            , timeout = Nothing
            }

The `method` is sent as [`Http.Method.toString`](Http-Method#toString) gives its name, so
`UNKNOWN "PROPFIND"` sends `PROPFIND`.

The `timeout` is how many milliseconds to wait for the final response's headers before the
request fails with `Http.Timeout`. It is rounded to whole milliseconds, at least 1, and
`Nothing`, or a value of 0 or less, means no timeout. On the JavaScript backend a timeout above
2147483647 milliseconds fails the request after 1 millisecond.

A header in `headers` whose name is empty or holds a CR, LF or `:`, or whose value holds a CR or
LF, is not sent. On the JavaScript backend a header that Node rejects, such as one whose name holds
a space, is not sent either.
values.type: { method : Http.Method.Method, headers : List.List Http.Header, url : String.String, body : Http.Stream.Body, expect : Http.Stream.Expect msg, timeout : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Float } -> Platform.Cmd.Cmd msg

values.name: streamBody
values.comment:
Makes a body that sends what is read from a stream, sent with the
[MIME type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_type) `mimeType` as its `Content-Type` (an empty
`mimeType` is treated as [`Body`](#Body) describes). The stream is sent as it is read, so
something large, like a file, can be sent without holding it all in memory:

    upload : Stream.Readable Bytes -> Cmd Msg
    upload fileStream =
        Http.Stream.request
            { method = PUT
            , headers = []
            , url = "https://example.com/upload"
            , body = Http.Stream.streamBody "text/csv" fileStream
            , expect = Http.Stream.expectStream Uploaded
            , timeout = Nothing
            }

The end of the stream is the end of the body. The request reads the stream through a pipe, so
the stream is locked, as [`Stream`](Stream) describes, while the request runs. A stream that is
already locked when the request is sent makes the request fail at once with `Http.NetworkError`
(on the JavaScript backend, a bad URL is reported first).

If the stream fails, because it is cancelled from its writing side or the resource behind it
fails, a transfer still running is stopped: before the response headers the request fails with
`Http.NetworkError`, and after them a read of the response body fails with `Stream.Failed`, which
[`fromStreamFailure`](#fromStreamFailure) reads as `Http.NetworkError`.
If instead the transfer ends before the whole stream has been sent (the response is complete,
the request has failed, or it was stopped), the rest is not sent, and the stream is cancelled,
at the latest when it next has a value to send. A 307 or 308 redirect fails with
`Http.NetworkError`, because a stream cannot be sent twice. Other redirects differ between
backends: on the JavaScript backend a 303, or a 301 or 302 after a `POST`, is followed as a `GET`
without a body and any other fails with `Http.NetworkError`; on the native backend such a request
can wait until its `timeout`, so set one.

values.name: streamResolver
values.comment:
Makes a [`Resolver`](#Resolver) that turns the `Http.Response` into the task's result with
`toResult`. As with [`expectStreamResponse`](#expectStreamResponse), a response of any status
code comes with its body stream.
values.type: (Http.Response (Stream.Readable Bytes.Bytes) -> Result.Result x a) -> Http.Stream.Resolver x a

values.name: stringBody
values.comment:
Makes a body holding `value` encoded as UTF-8, sent with the
[MIME type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_type) `mimeType` as its `Content-Type` (an empty
`mimeType` is treated as [`Body`](#Body) describes).

A lone surrogate in `value` is not valid in UTF-8, and the two backends differ: it is sent as
U+FFFD (the bytes `EF BF BD`) on the JavaScript backend, and in its 3-byte surrogate form on the
native backend.

values.name: task
values.comment:
Makes a `Task` that sends the request, as [`request`](#request) does, and succeeds or fails
with what `resolver` makes of the response. A task can be chained with other tasks, for
example opening a file stream first and then uploading it.

A task is also the way to cancel a request: run it in a process started with `Process.spawn`,
and stop that process with `Process.kill` before the response headers arrive, which stops the
transfer. Killing the process after the task has received the response does not stop the
transfer; cancel the body stream with `Stream.cancelReadable` instead (which fails with
`Locked` while a read is waiting on the body stream, or a pipe is reading it).
values.type: { method : Http.Method.Method, headers : List.List Http.Header, url : String.String, body : Http.Stream.Body, resolver : Http.Stream.Resolver x a, timeout : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Float } -> Task.Task x a

name: Path
comment:
A program needs to name files and directories before it can act on them, and this module
builds, prints and combines those names without touching the file system, in POSIX or Windows
syntax. The functions in [FileSystem](FileSystem) act on what a path names.

A [Path](#Path) is the text of a path split into parts: a _root_, which is what the path starts
from (`""` for a path relative to the current directory, `"/"` for an absolute POSIX path, or a
Windows prefix such as `C:\` or `\\server\share\`), then the directory entries, then the last
entry, split into a filename and an extension.

Because nothing here looks at a disk, paths are a lexical model, and two facts follow.

Parsing normalizes the text alone. `..` cancels the entry before it as text, so `"a/../b"` gives
the same path as `"b"` whether or not `a` exists or is a link. Repeated separators are dropped,
and so are `.` entries, except a leading `./` in POSIX syntax.

Parsing loses information. A trailing separator and a trailing dot are dropped (`"a."` prints as
`"a"`), and [toPosixString](#toPosixString) prints any Windows root as `/`. Printing a parsed
path does not always give back the text it came from.

A third fact is about the type: a `Path` is a record alias, so any record of its shape is a
path, and only the paths that [fromPosixString](#fromPosixString) and
[fromWin32String](#fromWin32String) return are sure to be normalized, apart from a last entry
`...`, which [fromPosixString](#fromPosixString) describes.

Elsewhere in this package a path reaches the operating system only as text printed by
[toPosixString](#toPosixString), and paths coming back are parsed with
[fromPosixString](#fromPosixString). A path parsed from Windows syntax therefore reaches the
file system with its drive or share printed as `/`.

[append](#append), [prepend](#prepend) and [join](#join) combine paths by their entries. The
result keeps the root of the path whose entries come first in it and discards the other root, so
adding an absolute path onto another does not start over from its root.

Most of this file is the Windows parser. Windows syntax has more kinds of root than POSIX: drives,
drive-relative paths (`C:foo`), UNC shares and device paths (`\\?\C:\x`, `\\.\COM1:`). It also
reserves device names such as `CON` and `NUL`, and the parser marks some relative paths with a
leading `.\`; [fromWin32String](#fromWin32String) says which.

@docs Path

aliases.name: Path
aliases.comment:
A file system path, split into the parts that both POSIX and Windows syntax have.

`root` is what the path starts from: `""` for a path relative to the current directory, `"/"`
for an absolute POSIX path, and for a Windows path its prefix together with the separator after
it, such as `C:\`, `\` or `\\server\share\`. A Windows path relative to a drive's current
directory, such as `C:foo`, has the root `C:`. A device path with a single entry, such as
`\\.\x`, is all root, with no separator after it.

`filename` and `extension` together are the last entry, which may name a directory as well as a
file. The extension is stored without its dot. Both are empty when the path has no last entry,
as for a path that is only a root.

Any record of this shape is a `Path`, since this is a record alias. Only the paths that
[fromPosixString](#fromPosixString) and [fromWin32String](#fromWin32String) return are sure to
be normalized, apart from a last entry `...`, which [fromPosixString](#fromPosixString)
describes.
aliases.type: { root : String.String, directory : List.List String.String, filename : String.String, extension : String.String }

values.name: append
values.comment:
Returns the second path with the first added at its end, which is [prepend](#prepend) with
the arguments swapped. The second path is the base, so `base |> append child` reads in order.

    append (fromPosixString "file.md") (fromPosixString "/home/me")
        |> toPosixString
        -- returns "/home/me/file.md"

The result keeps the base's root and discards the first path's, so appending an absolute path
does not replace the base.

values.name: appendPosixString
values.comment:
Parses the string with [fromPosixString](#fromPosixString) and [append](#append)s it to the
path.

values.name: appendWin32String
values.comment:
Parses the string with [fromWin32String](#fromWin32String) and [append](#append)s it to the
path.

values.name: empty
values.comment:
The path with no root and no entries, which both printers print as `"."`, the current
directory.

Parsing `""` or `"."` gives this path.

values.name: filenameWithExtension
values.comment:
Returns the last entry of a path: its filename, followed by a dot and the extension when
there is one.

    "/home/me/file.md"
        |> fromPosixString
        |> filenameWithExtension
        -- returns "file.md"

values.name: fromPosixString
values.comment:
Parses a path in POSIX syntax, where only `/` separates entries and a leading `/` is the root.

The result is normalized, except for the last case below. Repeated separators, a trailing
separator and `.` entries are dropped, and each `..` cancels the entry before it, so `"a/../b"`
gives the same path as `"b"`. A `..` with nothing before it to cancel is dropped from an absolute
path (`"/../a"` gives `"/a"`) and kept in a relative one (`"../a"`). `""`, `"."` and
`"a/.."` give [empty](#empty).

A leading `./` is the one `.` entry that is kept, as a `"."` directory entry, so `"./a"` prints
back as `"./a"`.

The extension is what follows the last dot of the last entry. An entry has none when it has no
dot, when its last dot is its first character (`".bashrc"`), or when it is `".."`. A trailing
dot gives an empty extension and is lost: `"a."` gives the filename `"a"`, and a last entry
`...` becomes `..`, so `"/x/..."` prints as `"/x/.."`, which names a different directory.

values.name: fromWin32String
values.comment:
Parses a path in Windows syntax, where both `\` and `/` separate entries.

The root is the path's prefix with the separator after it: a drive (`C:\`, or `C:` in the
drive-relative `C:foo\bar.txt`), a lone `\`, a UNC share (`\\server\share\`) or a device path
(`\\?\C:\`). A device path with a single entry, such as `\\.\x`, is all root, with no separator
after it.

The result is normalized as [fromPosixString](#fromPosixString) normalizes, except that a leading
`.\` is dropped too (`.\a\b` gives `a\b`), and the extension is split off the same way.

A path with no root gets a `"."` first directory entry, so that it prints with a leading `.\`,
when a colon ends an entry (`foo:`), when the normalized path would start with a drive
(`x\..\c:`), when the text before the first colon, as written, is a reserved device name in any
mix of upper and lower case (`CON:`, `COM1:x`), and, in a path with no colon, when the text as
written without its last character is a reserved name (`NULL`, `COM10`, `CONx`), unless that last
character lies outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, as an emoji does. These checks come before
`..` is resolved, so `x\..\CON:a` gives the unmarked `CON:a`. A bare `CON` or `CON.txt` is not
marked.

values.name: join
values.comment:
Combines the paths of a list from first to last, [append](#append)ing each to the result so
far. An empty list gives [empty](#empty).

The result keeps the root of the first path and discards the roots of the others.

values.name: parent
values.comment:
Returns the path of the directory that holds a path's last entry, or `Nothing` for
[empty](#empty) and for a path that is only a root.

    "/home/me/file.md"
        |> fromPosixString
        |> parent
        |> Maybe.map toPosixString
        -- returns Just "/home/me"

This is lexical: the parent of `"a"` is [empty](#empty), and so is the parent of `".."`.

The last directory entry becomes the result's last entry, split into a filename and an extension
only when it has exactly one dot, at that dot. For some entries this differs from
[fromPosixString](#fromPosixString): `.bashrc` gets the filename `""` and the extension
`"bashrc"`, and `a.b.c` gets no extension. These two print the same as the parsed parent but are
different records. An entry whose one dot is its last character loses the dot, so the parent of
`/x/a./f` prints as `/x/a`. The entry `a.b.` keeps its trailing dot, which parsing drops: the
parent of `/x/a.b./f` prints as `/x/a.b.`, and `fromPosixString "/x/a.b."` prints as `/x/a.b`.

A path with directory entries and an empty last entry, such as
`append empty (fromPosixString "/a/b")`, has its last directory entry moved into the last entry,
so its parent prints the same as the path itself, unless that entry ends in its only dot, which
the paragraph above says is lost.

values.name: prepend
values.comment:
Returns the second path with the first put in front of it.

The result has the first path's root. Its directory is the first path's directory entries and
last entry, then the second path's directory entries, with empty entries left out, and its last
entry is the second path's. The second path's root is discarded, so the prepended path of
`/home/me` and `/etc/x` is `/home/me/etc/x`.

The entries are not normalized again: a `.` or `..` entry of the second path stays where it is.

values.name: prependPosixString
values.comment:
Parses the string with [fromPosixString](#fromPosixString) and [prepend](#prepend)s it to the
path.

values.name: prependWin32String
values.comment:
Parses the string with [fromWin32String](#fromWin32String) and [prepend](#prepend)s it to the
path.

values.name: toPosixString
values.comment:
Prints a path in POSIX syntax, with `/` between the entries.

[empty](#empty) prints as `"."`. A root other than `""` and `"/"`, such as a Windows drive or
share, prints as `/`, so the Windows path `C:\a\b` prints as `/a/b`, and the drive-relative
`C:foo` prints as the absolute `/foo`.

values.name: toWin32String
values.comment:
Prints a path in Windows syntax, with `\` between the entries.

[empty](#empty) prints as `"."`. The root is printed as it is, so a POSIX root stays `/`: the
POSIX path `/a/b` prints as `/a\b`.

name: Socket
comment:
Whatever made a stream socket, TCP, Unix domain or TLS, the program uses it in the same way,
and this module is that common part: connections, listeners, name lookup and the socket error.

A [`Connection`](#Connection) is two byte streams, one carrying what the peer sends and one
carrying what is sent to it. Making a connection or a listener depends on its kind, and each
kind has its own module for that:

  - [`Socket.Tcp`](Socket-Tcp) connects to and listens on IPv4 and IPv6 addresses;
  - [`Socket.Unix`](Socket-Unix) connects to and listens on Unix domain socket paths;
  - [`Socket.Tls`](Socket-Tls) adds TLS encryption to TCP.

[`Socket.Udp`](Socket-Udp) sends and receives datagrams instead of streams, but its failures
are this module's [`Error`](#Error) too. Addresses and endpoints are described in
[`Socket.Address`](Socket-Address). Several of these modules define functions with the same
names, such as `close` and `listen`, so import them qualified:

    import Socket
    import Socket.Tcp

Once a connection exists, everything that happens to its data happens on its streams, and a
failure there is a `Stream.Error`, as the [`Stream`](Stream) module describes. When the
connection itself fails, a read or write fails with `Stream.Failed`, and
[`fromStreamFailure`](#fromStreamFailure) reads that failure back as an [`Error`](#Error); a
connection reset, for example, is a read whose failure has the kind
[`ConnectionReset`](#ErrorKind). This module's `Error` is otherwise for tasks such as
connecting, listening, accepting and looking up names.
Ending one direction only, by closing the writable while the readable stays open, is a
_half-close_: the peer reads to the end of the data and can still reply. A connection is
released once both of its streams have ended, or at once by [`close`](#close) or
[`reset`](#reset); a connection that the program simply forgets is not closed for it. An open connection on which no operation is waiting does not keep the
program running; an open [`Listener`](#Listener) keeps it running only while an
[`accept`](#accept) is waiting or an [`onConnection`](#onConnection) subscription exists. Held
connections do not keep it running.

A listener hands out the connections that clients make to it, through [`accept`](#accept) and
[`onConnection`](#onConnection), by one rule. A new connection goes to the oldest waiting
`accept` (a _parked_ accept); if there is none, to every `onConnection` subscription to that
listener, all of which receive the same `Connection`; and if there is neither, it is _held_
until the next `accept` or subscription, which takes the held connections oldest first. Where a
held connection waits depends on the backend. On the JavaScript backend the kernel accepts every
connection at once and holds up to the listener's `backlog`, at least 1 (511 for a Unix domain
listener), closing the newest beyond that. On the native backend a listener accepts only while
an `accept` is parked or a subscription exists, so a connection that arrives while there is
neither waits in the operating system's listen queue.

On native Windows, sockets are not supported: lookup, connecting and listening fail with
[`NotSupported`](#ErrorKind), and an `onConnection` subscription is a fatal error.

@docs lookup


## Errors

[`Error`](#Error) is the failure of the transports: TCP, Unix domain sockets and UDP. A program
matches on its [`ErrorKind`](#ErrorKind), so that it need not depend on the exact code an
operating system or a backend uses. TLS and WebSocket are protocols layered on a socket, and
each has its own error type that wraps this one: [`Socket.Tls.Error`](Socket-Tls#Error) and
[`WebSocket.Error`](WebSocket#Error).

@docs Error, ErrorKind, errorKind, errorToString, fromStreamFailure

unions.name: ErrorKind
unions.comment:
What kind of failure an [`Error`](#Error) is.

Most kinds stand for an operating system error, whose name is given in parentheses. Which name a
failure gets can depend on the operating system and the backend, and a kind may stand for more
than one of them, so that a program need not tell them apart.

  - `ConnectionRefused`: nothing listens at the address connected to (ECONNREFUSED). For a Unix
    domain socket, a socket file exists at the path but nobody listens on it.
  - `ConnectionReset`: the peer reset the connection or is gone (ECONNRESET, EPIPE). A connection
    that is reset after it has been handed out fails on its streams instead, with a failure that
    [`fromStreamFailure`](#fromStreamFailure) reads as this kind.
  - `TimedOut`: the operation took too long (ETIMEDOUT), for example a connect that ran past its
    `timeout`.
  - `NetworkUnreachable`: no route leads to the network or the host (ENETUNREACH,
    EHOSTUNREACH).
  - `AddressInUse`: the address is already in use (EADDRINUSE), for example by another listener.
    For a Unix domain socket, something already exists at the path.
  - `AddressNotAvailable`: the address cannot be used here (EADDRNOTAVAIL, EAFNOSUPPORT): it
    does not belong to this machine, or its address family cannot be used, as when an IPv6
    destination is given to an IPv4 UDP socket.
  - `HostNotFound`: a host name could not be resolved (ENOTFOUND, EAI_FAIL).
  - `HostLookupTryAgain`: the resolver failed for now and the lookup may succeed if tried again
    (EAI_AGAIN).
  - `PermissionDenied`: the operating system refused the operation (EACCES, EPERM), for example
    listening on a privileged port, or broadcasting a UDP datagram without `broadcast = True`.
    A Unix domain socket path that cannot be used for lack of permission is an
    `AddressPathFailed` instead.
  - `Cancelled`: the operation was cancelled (ECANCELED), for example an [`accept`](#accept)
    whose listener was closed, or a read on a connection closed with [`close`](#close).
  - `Busy`: something else is using the resource (EBUSY), for example a stream that a waiting
    read or write holds.
  - `InvalidInput`: an argument cannot be used (EINVAL), for example the peer credentials of a
    connection that is not a Unix domain connection.
  - `NotSupported`: the operation is not supported here (ENOTSUP), for example any socket on
    native Windows, or reading peer credentials where the system cannot.
  - `MessageTooLarge`: a UDP datagram is too large to send (EMSGSIZE).
  - `ListenQueueFull`: the operating system's queue of connections waiting on a listener is full
    (EAGAIN), as when connecting to a Unix domain socket on Linux.
  - `AddressPathFailed kind`: a Unix domain socket's path failed as a file path would, with the
    [`FileSystem.ErrorKind`](FileSystem#ErrorKind) it would have there:
    `NoSuchFileOrDirectory` (ENOENT: nothing at the path on connect, a missing parent directory
    on listen), `NotADirectory` (ENOTDIR), `LinkLoop` (ELOOP), `ReadOnlyFileSystem` (EROFS),
    `PathTooLong` (ENAMETOOLONG: longer than 107 bytes on Linux, 103 on macOS), or
    `PermissionDenied` (EACCES on the socket file or its directory).
  - `ConnectionTakenOver`: the connection's streams were taken over by another owner, such as
    `WebSocket.receiveUpgrade`; only stream failures have this kind.
  - `OtherSocketError code`: any other failure, with its code as the backend reports it, usually
    the name of an operating system error.

aliases.name: Connection
aliases.comment:
An open stream connection to a peer, over TCP, a Unix domain socket or TLS.

A connection is made by `Socket.Tcp.connect`, `Socket.Tcp.connectToHost`, `Socket.Unix.connect`
or `Socket.Tls.connect`, or received from a [`Listener`](#Listener). Read what the peer sends
from [`readable`](#readable) and send by writing to [`writable`](#writable). On a TLS
connection both streams carry the plaintext, and their failures are read with
[`Socket.Tls.fromStreamFailure`](Socket-Tls#fromStreamFailure), which also covers the failures
of the connection under TLS.
aliases.type: Socket.Internal.Connection

aliases.name: Error
aliases.comment:
A failed socket operation: what kind of failure it was, and a message for people to read.

This is the error of the transports: this module, [`Socket.Tcp`](Socket-Tcp),
[`Socket.Unix`](Socket-Unix) and [`Socket.Udp`](Socket-Udp). TCP, Unix domain sockets and UDP
are alternative transports that share one connection type and the functions of this module, so
they share this one error, and each of them meets only some of its kinds.

Protocols layered on a socket have their own error types, which wrap this one:
[`Socket.Tls.Error`](Socket-Tls#Error) has a `SocketError` case for failures below TLS, and
[`WebSocket.Error`](WebSocket#Error) one for failures below the WebSocket. `Http.Server.Error`,
the failure to start a server, is a separate type.

Read the kind with [`errorKind`](#errorKind) and the description with
[`errorToString`](#errorToString).
aliases.type: Socket.Internal.Error

aliases.name: Listener
aliases.comment:
A socket that receives the connections clients make to an address or a Unix domain socket
path. A listener is made by `Socket.Tcp.listen`, `Socket.Unix.listen` or `Socket.Tls.listen`, and
its connections are handed out by [`accept`](#accept) and [`onConnection`](#onConnection) as
the module documentation describes.

An open listener keeps the program running only while an `accept` on it is waiting or an
`onConnection` subscription to it exists.
aliases.type: Socket.Internal.Listener

values.name: accept
values.comment:
Waits for the listener's next connection.

A held connection, the oldest first, is returned at once. Otherwise the task is parked, and a
new connection goes to the oldest parked `accept` before any [`onConnection`](#onConnection)
subscription sees it.

Fails with [`Cancelled`](#ErrorKind) when the listener is closed while the task waits, and at
once on a listener that is already closed. A TLS listener closes a client whose handshake fails
without handing it out, so `accept` never fails because of TLS.

values.name: close
values.comment:
Closes the connection at once, without waiting for either stream to end.

Reads and writes waiting on its streams fail with `Stream.Failed`, a failure whose
[`Error`](#Error) has the kind [`Cancelled`](#ErrorKind), and so do later ones on a stream that
had not already ended. Bytes still queued in the writable are
dropped; the socket is closed, and what the operating system has already taken is left to it to
send. On Linux a socket closed with received data that was never read sends the peer a reset
instead of the end of the data. A TLS connection is closed without a TLS `close_notify`.

Closing a connection that is already closed does nothing. For an orderly end, close the
[`writable`](#writable) and read the [`readable`](#readable) to its end instead.

values.name: closeListener
values.comment:
Stops listening.

Parked [`accept`](#accept) tasks fail with [`Cancelled`](#ErrorKind), and connections the listener received
but has not handed out are closed. Connections already handed out stay open. The task succeeds
once the listening socket has been closed, so the address can be listened on again at once; a
Unix domain listener removes its socket file first.

Closing a listener that is already closed does nothing.

values.name: errorKind
values.comment:
Returns the kind of the error.

    case Socket.errorKind error of
        Socket.ConnectionRefused ->
            "nobody is listening"

        Socket.TimedOut ->
            "no answer in time"

        _ ->
            Socket.errorToString error

values.name: errorToString
values.comment:
Returns a description of the error for people to read: the code the backend reported,
`": "`, and the message, as in `"ECONNREFUSED: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4000"`.

values.name: fromStreamFailure
values.comment:
Reads the failure of a socket connection's stream back as an [`Error`](#Error), or returns
`Nothing` for a failure that some other kind of stream made.

A read or write on a connection's [`readable`](#readable) or [`writable`](#writable) that fails
because of the connection fails with `Stream.Failed`, and this gives its error, for example:

  - the kind [`ConnectionReset`](#ErrorKind) when the peer reset the connection or is gone;
  - [`Cancelled`](#ErrorKind) after [`close`](#close) or [`reset`](#reset);
  - [`ConnectionTakenOver`](#ErrorKind) once `WebSocket.receiveUpgrade` has taken the
    connection over.

    case error of
        Stream.Failed failure ->
            case Socket.fromStreamFailure failure of
                Just socketError ->
                    Socket.errorToString socketError

                Nothing ->
                    Stream.failureToString failure

        _ ->
            Stream.errorToString error

On a TLS connection, use [`Socket.Tls.fromStreamFailure`](Socket-Tls#fromStreamFailure), which
reads both the failures of TLS and those of the connection under it.

values.name: listenerEndpoint
values.comment:
Returns the endpoint the listener is bound to. For a listener on port 0, its port is the one
the operating system chose.

values.name: localEndpoint
values.comment:
Returns this end of the connection, as it was when the connection was made.

On a Unix domain connection the server side's local endpoint is the path its listener listens on,
and the client side's is the empty path. An IP address whose text from the kernel does not parse
becomes the unspecified address; for example, on the JavaScript backend an address Node does not
report is `0.0.0.0` with port 0.

values.name: lookup
values.comment:
Looks up the IP addresses of a host name, in the order the system resolver returns them,
with duplicates removed.

    Socket.lookup "localhost"

An IP address literal such as `"127.0.0.1"` gives that address. A name with no addresses fails
with [`HostNotFound`](#ErrorKind), and so does `""`, without asking the resolver. A temporary
failure of the resolver fails with [`HostLookupTryAgain`](#ErrorKind).

values.name: onConnection
values.comment:
Creates a subscription to the connections the listener receives that no parked
[`accept`](#accept) takes, including those held before the subscription started.

    subscriptions : Model -> Sub Msg
    subscriptions model =
        Socket.onConnection model.listener GotConnection

Every subscription to the same listener receives the same `Connection`, and so the same
streams, so subscribe once per listener. A subscription to a closed listener never fires.

values.name: readable
values.comment:
Returns the stream of bytes the peer sends. A read fails with `Stream.Closed` once the peer
has finished sending and everything it sent has been read.

A read that fails because of the connection fails with `Stream.Failed`, and
[`fromStreamFailure`](#fromStreamFailure) gives the [`Error`](#Error): for example the kind
[`ConnectionReset`](#ErrorKind) when the peer reset the connection, [`Cancelled`](#ErrorKind)
after [`close`](#close) or [`reset`](#reset), and [`ConnectionTakenOver`](#ErrorKind) once
`WebSocket.receiveUpgrade` has taken the connection over.

values.name: remoteEndpoint
values.comment:
Returns the peer's end of the connection, as it was when the connection was made.

On a Unix domain connection the client side's remote endpoint is the path it connected to, and
the server side's is the empty path. As for [`localEndpoint`](#localEndpoint), an IP address whose
text from the kernel does not parse becomes the unspecified address.

values.name: reset
values.comment:
Aborts the connection: as [`close`](#close), except that a TCP or TLS connection is closed
with a TCP reset (RST), which discards whatever the operating system has not yet sent. On a Unix
domain connection this is the same as `close`.

values.name: writable
values.comment:
Returns the stream of bytes sent to the peer.

Closing it with `Stream.closeWritable` sends the end of the data (on a TLS connection, a TLS
`close_notify` and then the end of the data) once everything written before it has been passed
on, and leaves the readable open: a half-close. A write that fails because of the connection
fails with `Stream.Failed`, and [`fromStreamFailure`](#fromStreamFailure) gives the
[`Error`](#Error): for example the kind [`ConnectionReset`](#ErrorKind) when the peer is gone
(EPIPE), or [`Cancelled`](#ErrorKind) after [`close`](#close) or [`reset`](#reset).

name: Socket.Address
comment:
Many socket functions in this package take an IP address or the endpoint of a socket as a
value of this module rather than as text, and this module defines those values: IPv4 and IPv6
addresses, and the endpoints of sockets.

An [`Address`](#Address) is valid by construction. It is made only here: by parsing text with
[`fromString`](#fromString), from bytes with [`fromOctets`](#fromOctets), as one of the
well-known addresses, or with [`unmapIPv4`](#unmapIPv4). [`toString`](#toString) prints every
address in one canonical form, which `fromString` reads back as the same address. Parsing and
printing are pure Elm and never touch the network, so they behave the same on every platform
and backend.

Host names are not addresses: `fromString "localhost"` is `Nothing`. Resolve a name with
[`Socket.lookup`](Socket#lookup), or connect to one directly with
[`Socket.Tcp.connectToHost`](Socket-Tcp#connectToHost).

Four terms are used throughout.

An IPv6 address may carry a _scope_ (also called a zone): the text after a `%`, such as the `eth0`
of `fe80::1%eth0`, which names the network interface a link-local address belongs to. The scope
is part of the address, so `fe80::1%eth0` and `fe80::1` are not equal.

The _unspecified_ address, `0.0.0.0` or `::`, names no particular host. [`any`](#any) returns it.

An _IPv4-mapped_ address is an IPv6 address that carries an IPv4 address in its last 32 bits,
written `::ffff:a.b.c.d`. It is an IPv6 address and is not equal to the IPv4 address it carries;
[`unmapIPv4`](#unmapIPv4) returns that IPv4 address. A TCP listener or UDP socket on the
unspecified IPv6 address with `ipv6Only = False` sees its IPv4 peers this way.

An _endpoint_ is where a socket is: an address and a port, or the path of a Unix domain socket.

    Socket.Address.fromString "::FFFF:127.0.0.1"
        |> Maybe.map Socket.Address.toString
    --> Just "::ffff:127.0.0.1"


## Addresses

@docs Address, Family, fromString, toString, fromOctets, toOctets, family


## Well-known addresses

@docs loopback, any


## Classification

@docs isLoopback, isUnspecified, isIPv4Mapped, unmapIPv4


## Endpoints

@docs Endpoint, InetEndpoint

unions.name: Address
unions.comment:
An IPv4 or IPv6 address, valid by construction; an IPv6 address may also carry a scope.

A value is obtained from [`fromString`](#fromString), [`fromOctets`](#fromOctets),
[`loopback`](#loopback), [`any`](#any) or [`unmapIPv4`](#unmapIPv4), so every `Address` is valid:
[`toString`](#toString) prints it as text that `fromString` reads back as the same address.

Two addresses are equal (`==`) when they have the same family, the same bits and the same scope
text, compared exactly. An IPv4-mapped address is therefore never equal to the IPv4 address it
carries, and `fe80::1%eth0` is not equal to `fe80::1%ETH0`.

unions.name: Endpoint
unions.comment:
Where a stream socket is: one end of a connection, or the place a listener listens.

`Inet` carries an IP address and a port.

`Unix` carries the path of a Unix domain socket. The [empty path](Path#empty) stands for an
unnamed socket: a connection made with `Socket.Unix` has it as its local endpoint, and a
connection accepted by a Unix listener has it as its remote endpoint.

unions.name: Family
unions.comment:
Which of the two kinds of address a value is: `IPv4`, 32 bits, or `IPv6`, 128 bits. An
IPv4-mapped address is `IPv6`.

aliases.name: InetEndpoint
aliases.comment:
An IP address and a port number.

`port_` has its underscore because `port` is a reserved word in Elm. It is a plain `Int`, and
the type does not restrict it to the port range 0–65535.
aliases.type: { address : Socket.Address.Address, port_ : Basics.Int }

values.name: any
values.comment:
Returns the unspecified address of a family, `0.0.0.0` or `::`.

As the address to listen or bind on, it stands for every local interface rather than one.
Whether the IPv6 one also takes IPv4 traffic is set by `ipv6Only` in
[`Socket.Tcp.ListenOptions`](Socket-Tcp#ListenOptions) and
[`Socket.Udp.BindOptions`](Socket-Udp#BindOptions). [`Http.Server`](Http-Server) has no
`ipv6Only` and listens as if it were `False`.

values.name: family
values.comment:
Returns the family of an address. An IPv4-mapped address such as `"::ffff:127.0.0.1"` is an IPv6
address; [`unmapIPv4`](#unmapIPv4) turns it into an IPv4 one.

values.name: fromOctets
values.comment:
Builds an address from its bytes in network order: 4 values give an IPv4 address and 16 values
an IPv6 address (without a scope). Any other length, or a value outside 0–255, gives `Nothing`.

    fromOctets [ 127, 0, 0, 1 ] |> Maybe.map toString
    --> Just "127.0.0.1"

values.name: fromString
values.comment:
Parses the text of an IPv4 or IPv6 address, giving `Nothing` for anything that is not one.

  - **IPv4:** four decimal fields from 0 to 255, separated by dots, each of 1 to 3 ASCII digits.
    A leading zero is not allowed (`"01.2.3.4"` is rejected).
  - **IPv6:** the text form of RFC 4291: groups of 1 to 4 hexadecimal digits (in either case)
    separated by colons, at most one `::` standing for one or more zero groups, and optionally a
    dotted IPv4 address, written as above, in place of the last two groups
    (`"::ffff:192.0.2.1"`). Without `::` there must be exactly 8 groups; with it, at most 7. A
    dotted ending counts as two groups.
  - An IPv6 address may end in a scope: `%` followed by 1 to 15 characters from `A-Z`, `a-z`,
    `0-9`, `_`, `.` and `-`, such as the interface name `"eth0"` or the interface number `"2"`.
    An IPv4 address cannot have a scope.

Anything else, including surrounding whitespace, gives `Nothing`.

    fromString "localhost"
    --> Nothing

values.name: isIPv4Mapped
values.comment:
Returns `True` for IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses (`::ffff:0:0/96`), such as `::ffff:127.0.0.1`,
whatever their scope.

values.name: isLoopback
values.comment:
Returns `True` for loopback addresses: `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`, and the IPv4-mapped forms of
`127.0.0.0/8` (such as `::ffff:127.0.0.1`). The scope is ignored.

values.name: isUnspecified
values.comment:
Returns `True` for the unspecified addresses `0.0.0.0` and `::`. The scope is ignored. Unlike
[`isLoopback`](#isLoopback), this does not look inside an IPv4-mapped address: `::ffff:0.0.0.0`
is not unspecified.

values.name: loopback
values.comment:
Returns the loopback address of a family, `127.0.0.1` or `::1`, the address by which a host
reaches itself. [`isLoopback`](#isLoopback) accepts more addresses than these two.

values.name: toOctets
values.comment:
Returns the bytes of an address in network order: 4 for IPv4, 16 for IPv6. The scope is not
included.

values.name: toString
values.comment:
Prints an address in its canonical form, which [`fromString`](#fromString) reads back as the
same address.

  - IPv4: dotted decimal, `"127.0.0.1"`.
  - IPv6 (RFC 5952): lower-case hexadecimal without leading zeros; the longest run of two or more
    zero groups (the leftmost one if there is a tie) is written `::`, and a single zero group is
    written `0`. IPv4-mapped addresses are written `"::ffff:a.b.c.d"`. The scope, if any, follows
    after a `%`.

```
fromString "2001:DB8:0:0:1:0:0:1" |> Maybe.map toString
--> Just "2001:db8::1:0:0:1"
```

values.name: unmapIPv4
values.comment:
Turns an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address into the IPv4 address it carries (`::ffff:127.0.0.1` becomes
`127.0.0.1`), dropping any scope. Every other address is returned unchanged.

name: Socket.Tcp
comment:
A TCP connection or listener is made from an IP address and a port, and this module makes
them. Once made, it is an ordinary [`Socket.Connection`](Socket#Connection) or
[`Socket.Listener`](Socket#Listener), used through [`Socket`](Socket) like a connection or
listener of any other kind.

Addresses are [`Socket.Address.Address`](Socket-Address#Address) values, IPv4 or IPv6, not text,
so a host name has to be resolved before anything connects to it. [`connect`](#connect) takes an
address; [`connectToHost`](#connectToHost) takes text, either an address literal, used as it is,
or a host name, which it resolves with [`Socket.lookup`](Socket#lookup) first. A server
[`listen`](#listen)s on an address and gets its connections from
[`Socket.accept`](Socket#accept) or [`Socket.onConnection`](Socket#onConnection), by the rule the
`Socket` module describes.

What this module offers for a connection that already exists is two TCP options: Nagle's
algorithm, which holds back small writes to send them together, and keep-alive probes, which
the operating system sends on an idle connection to find out whether the peer is still there.
Both can be chosen when connecting and changed later with [`setNoDelay`](#setNoDelay) and
[`setKeepAlive`](#setKeepAlive).

Times are given in milliseconds, as `Maybe Int`, and the two fields of `ConnectOptions` that
take one read a non-positive value differently. A connect `timeout` of `Just 0` or less is no
timeout, the same as `Nothing`. A `keepAlive` of `Just 0` or less turns keep-alive on, at 1
second; only `Nothing` leaves it off.

[`Socket.Tls`](Socket-Tls) takes the same [`ConnectOptions`](#ConnectOptions) and
[`ListenOptions`](#ListenOptions) for the TCP side of its connections and listeners.

    import Socket
    import Socket.Address as Address exposing (Family(..))
    import Socket.Tcp

    listener =
        Socket.Tcp.listen (Socket.Tcp.defaultListenOptions (Address.loopback IPv4) 8080)


## Connecting

@docs ConnectOptions, defaultConnectOptions, connect, connectToHost


## Listening

@docs ListenOptions, defaultListenOptions, listen


## Connection options

@docs setNoDelay, setKeepAlive

aliases.name: ConnectOptions
aliases.comment:
One attempt to open a TCP connection: where to connect, how long to wait, and the TCP
options the connection starts with.

  - `timeout`, up to 2147483647 (about 24.8 days), is the most time, in milliseconds, to wait
    until the connection is established (and, for `Socket.Tls.connect`, until the TLS handshake
    is done as well); the attempt then fails with
    [`Socket.TimedOut`](Socket#ErrorKind). `Nothing`, or `Just n` with
    `n <= 0`, waits as long as the operating system does.
  - `noDelay = True` turns Nagle's algorithm off (`TCP_NODELAY`), so small writes are sent at
    once.
  - `keepAlive` is how long, in milliseconds, the connection must be idle before keep-alive
    probes are sent, within any limit the operating system sets (32767 seconds on Linux). It
    is rounded up to whole seconds, at least 1 second, so `Just 0` or a negative value sends
    probes after 1 second. `Nothing` sends none.

Setting `noDelay` and `keepAlive` here is best effort: if the operating system refuses one, the
connection is still made.
aliases.type: { address : Socket.Address.Address, port_ : Basics.Int, timeout : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int, noDelay : Basics.Bool, keepAlive : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int }

aliases.name: ListenOptions
aliases.comment:
Where a TCP listener listens, which connections it accepts, and how it queues the ones it has
not handed out yet.

  - `port_` 0 lets the operating system pick a free port, which
    [`Socket.listenerEndpoint`](Socket#listenerEndpoint) then reports. The unspecified address
    ([`Socket.Address.any`](Socket-Address#any)) listens on every interface.
  - `backlog` is the length of the operating system's queue of connections waiting to be
    accepted, clamped to between 1 and 65535 (the operating system may limit it further). On the
    JavaScript backend it is also how many connections the listener holds for a later `accept`,
    as the `Socket` module describes.
  - `ipv6Only` matters only for an IPv6 address. When `False`, a listener on `any IPv6` also
    accepts IPv4 connections, whose addresses are then IPv4-mapped (see
    [`Socket.Address.unmapIPv4`](Socket-Address#unmapIPv4)). When `True`, it accepts IPv6
    connections only.

On the native backend the listening socket is made with `SO_REUSEADDR`, so the port can be
listened on again as soon as an earlier listener on it has closed.
aliases.type: { address : Socket.Address.Address, port_ : Basics.Int, backlog : Basics.Int, ipv6Only : Basics.Bool }

values.name: connect
values.comment:
Opens a TCP connection, succeeding once the connection is established.

    Socket.Tcp.connect (Socket.Tcp.defaultConnectOptions (Address.loopback IPv4) 8080)

Fails with, for example, [`Socket.ConnectionRefused`](Socket#ErrorKind) when nothing listens
there, [`Socket.TimedOut`](Socket#ErrorKind) when the `timeout` has passed, or
[`Socket.NetworkUnreachable`](Socket#ErrorKind) when no route leads to the address.

values.name: connectToHost
values.comment:
Opens a TCP connection to a host given by name, or by an address literal, and a port, with
the [default options](#defaultConnectOptions).

Text that [`Socket.Address.fromString`](Socket-Address#fromString) reads as an address, such as
`"127.0.0.1"` or `"::1"`, is used as it is. Anything else is resolved with
[`Socket.lookup`](Socket#lookup), and a failed lookup fails the task with its error. The
addresses found are tried one after the other, in the order `lookup` returns them, until one
connects. If every attempt fails, the task fails with the last attempt's error; a name without
addresses fails with [`Socket.HostNotFound`](Socket#ErrorKind).

    Socket.Tcp.connectToHost "localhost" 8080

The default options have no timeout, so each attempt waits as long as the operating system does
before the next address is tried. For a time limit on each attempt, resolve the name with
`Socket.lookup` and call [`connect`](#connect) with a `timeout`.

values.name: defaultConnectOptions
values.comment:
Returns options for connecting to `address` on `port_` with no timeout, Nagle's algorithm on
(`noDelay = False`) and no keep-alive.

values.name: defaultListenOptions
values.comment:
Returns options for listening on `address` and `port_` with a backlog of 511 and
`ipv6Only = False`.

values.name: listen
values.comment:
Starts listening for TCP connections, succeeding with the listener once it is bound and
listening. Fails with, for example, [`Socket.AddressInUse`](Socket#ErrorKind) when the address
and port are taken, [`Socket.PermissionDenied`](Socket#ErrorKind) for a privileged port, or
[`Socket.AddressNotAvailable`](Socket#ErrorKind) for an address that does not belong to this
machine.

values.name: setKeepAlive
values.comment:
Starts sending keep-alive probes once the connection has been idle for the given number of
milliseconds, within any limit the operating system sets (32767 seconds on Linux), or stops
sending them (`Nothing`). The time is rounded up to whole seconds, at least 1 second, so
`Just 0` or a negative value turns probes on at 1 second rather than off.

On a Unix domain connection, or one that has already been closed, this succeeds and does
nothing.

values.name: setNoDelay
values.comment:
Turns Nagle's algorithm off for the connection (`True`, so small writes are sent at once) or
on (`False`). On a Unix domain connection, or one that has already been closed, this succeeds
and does nothing.

name: Socket.Tls
comment:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts a TCP connection and lets a client check that it is
talking to the server it meant, and this module makes TLS connections and listeners. Once made,
a TLS connection is an ordinary [`Socket.Connection`](Socket#Connection) whose streams carry the
plaintext. The encryption happens underneath, and the program uses the connection through
[`Socket`](Socket) and its streams as it would any other.

A TLS connection starts with a _handshake_, in which the two ends agree on a TLS version and a
cipher, and the client, unless told not to, verifies the server's certificate. _Verification_
checks that the certificate was signed by an authority the client trusts and that it names the
server the client meant. [`Verification`](#Verification) says which authorities are trusted, and the
`serverName` of [`ClientOptions`](#ClientOptions) says which name the certificate must hold.

Two further things travel in the handshake. _SNI_ (Server Name Indication) is the client telling
the server the host name it wants, so that a server with several certificates can choose one.
_ALPN_ (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) is the client offering a list of application
protocols, such as `"h2"` and `"http/1.1"`, from which the server chooses one.

[`connect`](#connect) takes an address, not a host name, so resolving the name is the caller's
job, for example with [`Socket.lookup`](Socket#lookup). The server name is used only for TLS,
never to find the server. For example:

    Socket.lookup "example.com"
        |> Task.andThen
            (\addresses ->
                case addresses of
                    address :: _ ->
                        Socket.Tls.connect
                            (Socket.Tls.defaultClientOptions "example.com")
                            (Socket.Tcp.defaultConnectOptions address 443)

                    [] ->
                        Task.fail ...
            )

A server [`listen`](#listen)s and gets its connections from [`Socket.accept`](Socket#accept) or
[`Socket.onConnection`](Socket#onConnection), by the rule the `Socket` module describes. A
connection reaches that rule only once its handshake has succeeded, so a client whose handshake
is slow can be overtaken by clients that connected after it.

TLS is a protocol layered on a TCP connection, so this module has its own
[`Error`](#Error), which says in which layer a failure happened. A failure of the TCP connection
underneath is a `SocketError` holding a [`Socket.Error`](Socket#Error), as `Socket.Tcp` would
report it; a failure of TLS itself is a `TlsError` holding a [`Problem`](#Problem). A certificate
that fails verification makes `connect` fail with
`TlsError (CertificateRejected problem)`, where the
[`CertificateProblem`](#CertificateProblem) says what was wrong with it. A server that closes the
connection during the handshake is a failure of the connection, not of TLS: a `SocketError`
whose kind is [`Socket.ConnectionReset`](Socket#ErrorKind).

Once a connection has been made, failures to read or write arrive on its streams, as for any
connection, and [`fromStreamFailure`](#fromStreamFailure) reads them back as an `Error`.


## Clients

@docs ClientOptions, Verification, defaultClientOptions, connect


## Servers

@docs ServerOptions, listen


## Connection information

@docs Info, TlsVersion, info


## Errors

@docs Error, Problem, CertificateProblem, errorToString, fromStreamFailure

unions.name: CertificateProblem
unions.comment:
Why a client rejected a server's certificate. The code each case stands for, as the backends
report it, is in parentheses.

  - `Expired`: the certificate has expired (CERT_HAS_EXPIRED).
  - `NotYetValid`: the certificate is not valid yet (CERT_NOT_YET_VALID).
  - `Revoked`: the certificate was revoked (CERT_REVOKED).
  - `SelfSigned`: the certificate is self-signed and not trusted
    (DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT).
  - `SelfSignedInChain`: the chain ends in a self-signed certificate that is not trusted
    (SELF_SIGNED_CERT_IN_CHAIN).
  - `IssuerNotTrusted`: the certificate of the authority that signed it is not available or not
    trusted (UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY).
  - `LeafNotVerifiable`: the server's own certificate cannot be verified, usually because the
    server did not send the intermediate certificates (UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE).
  - `NameMismatch`: the certificate does not name the `serverName` connected to, as a DNS name
    or an IP address (ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID).
  - `VerificationFailed`: verification failed for another reason (CERT_VERIFY_FAILED on the
    native backend; on the JavaScript backend, any other verification code Node reports).

unions.name: Error
unions.comment:
A failed TLS operation, by the layer it failed in.

  - `SocketError error`: the TCP connection under TLS failed, or an argument of the TCP side
    could not be used; `error` is a [`Socket.Error`](Socket#Error), whose
    [`Socket.errorKind`](Socket#errorKind) says what went wrong, as for `Socket.Tcp`. A peer
    that drops the connection during the handshake is a `SocketError` with the kind
    [`Socket.ConnectionReset`](Socket#ErrorKind).
  - `TlsError problem`: TLS itself failed; the [`Problem`](#Problem) says how.

Only failures produced by TLS itself, such as a certificate check or an error that the TLS
library reports, are a `TlsError`.

unions.name: Problem
unions.comment:
How TLS itself failed.

  - `CertificateRejected problem`: `connect` rejected the server's certificate; the
