    [`CertificateProblem`](#CertificateProblem) says why.
  - `CertificateUnusable reason`: certificates or a key given to this module cannot be used: the
    `certificateChain` or `privateKey` of [`listen`](#listen), the two not belonging together, or
    the certificates of `TrustedCertificates` for `connect`. `reason` is the TLS library's reason
    in upper case with underscores, such as `"NO_CERTIFICATES"`; the backend reports it as the
    code `ERR_SSL_<reason>`.
  - `HandshakeFailed reason`: the handshake, or the TLS layer of an open connection, failed for
    another reason, such as the two ends sharing no TLS version or cipher. `reason` is the TLS
    library's reason as for `CertificateUnusable`, or `"UNKNOWN"` when the library gave none.

The reasons stay text because the TLS library has hundreds of them.

unions.name: TlsVersion
Verification
unions.comment:
Which authorities a client trusts to vouch for a server's certificate.

`SystemCertificates` trusts the operating system's certificate authorities. On the native
backend a non-empty `SSL_CERT_FILE` environment variable replaces them with the certificates in
the file it names, and a non-empty `SSL_CERT_DIR` replaces them with a directory of certificates
under OpenSSL's hashed file names (as `openssl rehash` makes them), together with the file when
both are set. On the JavaScript backend a non-empty `SSL_CERT_FILE` likewise replaces them with
the certificates in the file it names, and a non-empty `SSL_CERT_DIR` set as well adds back the
authorities Node reports as the system's. The variables and the system's authorities are read
when a connection first needs them, not for every connection.

`TrustedCertificates pem` trusts only the PEM-encoded certificates in `pem`, which may hold one
or more; the system's authorities are not consulted. On the native backend, reading stops at the
first certificate block that cannot be read, and the certificates after it are not trusted. When
no certificate can be read from `pem`, `connect` fails with
`TlsError (CertificateUnusable reason)` before it contacts the server.

`NoVerification` accepts any certificate and checks no name. The connection is encrypted, but
the server is not authenticated, so anyone able to intercept the connection can pose as it. It
is meant for testing.

aliases.name: ClientOptions
aliases.comment:
How a client secures a connection: the name the server's certificate must hold, the
authorities it trusts, and the application protocols it offers.

`serverName` is used only for TLS, never to find the server. A DNS name is sent as SNI and must
match the certificate. An IP address literal, such as `"192.0.2.1"`, is not sent and must match
one of the certificate's IP addresses. On the native backend an IPv6 literal with a zone, such as
`"fe80::1%eth0"`, counts as a DNS name. The empty string sends no name, and the certificate is
then checked against the trusted authorities but not against any name. With `NoVerification`
nothing is checked, though a DNS name is still sent.

`alpn` is the list of protocols to offer, such as `[ "h2", "http/1.1" ]`, and `[]` offers none.
The server chooses which one is used, and [`info`](#info) reports it. Each name must be 1 to 255
bytes of UTF-8, or `connect` fails with a `SocketError` whose kind is
[`Socket.InvalidInput`](Socket#ErrorKind).
aliases.type: { serverName : String.String, verification : Socket.Tls.Verification, alpn : List.List String.String }

aliases.name: Info
aliases.comment:
What a connection's TLS handshake agreed on.

`version` is the TLS version, a [`TlsVersion`](#TlsVersion). `alpn` is the application
protocol agreed, such as `Just "h2"`, and `Nothing` when none was agreed. `cipher` is the cipher
suite, in OpenSSL's name, such as `"TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384"`.
aliases.type: { version : Socket.Tls.TlsVersion, alpn : Maybe.Maybe String.String, cipher : String.String }

aliases.name: ServerOptions
aliases.comment:
What a TLS listener presents to its clients: its certificate and private key, and the
application protocols it supports.

`certificateChain` is PEM text holding the server's own certificate first, followed by any
intermediate certificates that link it to an authority. `privateKey` is the PEM-encoded key that
belongs to that certificate.

`alpn` is the list of protocols the server supports, in its order of preference. Of the
protocols a client offers, the server chooses the first in its own list, and when the client
offers none of them the handshake fails. A client that offers no protocols is served without
one, and `[]` ignores what clients offer. `Http.Server` does not use this field; it chooses its
protocols itself.
aliases.type: { certificateChain : String.String, privateKey : String.String, alpn : List.List String.String }

values.name: connect
values.comment:
Opens a TCP connection and secures it with TLS, succeeding once the handshake has finished
and, unless verification is off, the server's certificate has been accepted.

The TCP side is made from the same options as by `Socket.Tcp.connect`, and fails in the same
ways, as a `SocketError`. Its `timeout` covers the handshake too: the task fails with a
`SocketError` whose kind is [`Socket.TimedOut`](Socket#ErrorKind) when connecting and the
handshake together take longer. The `alpn` names, and the certificates of `TrustedCertificates`,
are checked before anything connects, so a problem with them fails the task without contacting
the server.

A failure of TLS itself is a `TlsError`: `CertificateRejected` when the server's certificate is
rejected, and `HandshakeFailed` when the handshake fails for another reason, for example when the
two ends share no TLS version or cipher. A server that closes the connection during the handshake
is a `SocketError` with the kind [`Socket.ConnectionReset`](Socket#ErrorKind).

values.name: defaultClientOptions
values.comment:
Returns options for a server named `serverName`, trusting the system's certificate
authorities (`SystemCertificates`) and offering no application protocols.

values.name: errorToString
values.comment:
Returns a description of the error for people to read. For a `SocketError` it is that of
[`Socket.errorToString`](Socket#errorToString). For a `TlsError` it is the code the backend
reports for the problem, `": "`, and a description of it, as in
`"CERT_HAS_EXPIRED: the certificate has expired"` or
`"ERR_SSL_NO_CERTIFICATES: the certificates cannot be used"`.

values.name: fromStreamFailure
values.comment:
Reads the failure of a TLS connection's stream back as an [`Error`](#Error), or returns
`Nothing` for a failure that some other kind of stream made.

A read or write on the streams of a TLS connection that fails because of the connection fails
with `Stream.Failed`. This gives a `TlsError` when TLS itself failed, for example with
`HandshakeFailed` when the peer sent data TLS cannot accept, and a `SocketError` when the
connection under TLS failed, with the same [`Socket.Error`](Socket#Error) that
[`Socket.fromStreamFailure`](Socket#fromStreamFailure) gives. One call covers both, so a
program reading a TLS connection needs only this one.

values.name: info
values.comment:
Returns what the handshake of a TLS connection agreed on.

Fails with a `SocketError` whose kind is [`Socket.InvalidInput`](Socket#ErrorKind) for a
connection that is not a TLS connection. Once the connection has ended, it may fail in the same
way.

values.name: listen
values.comment:
Starts listening for TLS connections, succeeding with the listener once it is bound and
listening. The TCP side is set up from the same options as by `Socket.Tcp.listen`, and fails in
the same ways, as a `SocketError`.

The certificate, the key, and whether the two belong together are checked before anything
listens. When they cannot be used, the task fails with `TlsError (CertificateUnusable reason)`.
An `alpn` name that is empty or longer than 255 bytes fails it with a `SocketError` whose kind
is [`Socket.InvalidInput`](Socket#ErrorKind).

A client whose handshake fails, or has not finished after 120 seconds, is closed without being
handed to the program. On the native backend at most 64 handshakes are under way at once on one
listener; further clients wait in the operating system's listen queue.

name: Socket.Udp
comment:
Some protocols exchange separate short messages rather than a stream of bytes, and UDP is
how such messages travel. This module provides UDP sockets, which send and receive datagrams over
IPv4 and IPv6.

A _datagram_ is one message: a sequence of bytes sent in one piece to an address and port. It
arrives whole or not at all, and the network may lose, duplicate or reorder datagrams without
telling either end. So datagrams here are values, not streams: [`send`](#send) takes one
`Bytes`, and [`receive`](#receive) and [`onMessage`](#onMessage) hand out one
[`Datagram`](#Datagram) at a time, with the endpoint it came from.

A [`Socket`](#Socket) is bound to one local address and port with [`bind`](#bind). The family
of that address, IPv4 or IPv6, is the socket's family. One socket can send to any number of
endpoints and receives the datagrams sent to its own endpoint. An open socket keeps the
program running only while a [`receive`](#receive) is waiting or an [`onMessage`](#onMessage)
subscription exists.

    import Socket
    import Socket.Address as Address exposing (Family(..))
    import Socket.Udp
    import Task exposing (Task)

    bindLoopback : Task Socket.Error Socket.Udp.Socket
    bindLoopback =
        Socket.Udp.bind (Socket.Udp.defaultBindOptions (Address.loopback IPv4) 0)

Arriving datagrams are handed out by one rule, the same one [`Socket`](Socket) describes for the
connections of a listener. A new datagram goes to the oldest waiting `receive`; if there is none,
to every `onMessage` subscription to that socket, all of which receive the same `Datagram`; and
if there is neither, it is _held_ until the next `receive` or subscription, which takes the held
datagrams oldest first. The kernel holds at most 64 datagrams per socket, and drops the oldest
beyond that. Where a datagram that nobody takes waits depends on the backend. On the JavaScript
backend every datagram is read as soon as it arrives, so it is held. On the native backend the
socket reads only while a `receive` is waiting or a subscription exists, so a datagram that
arrives while there is neither stays in the operating system's receive buffer.

A _multicast group_ is an IP address that stands for the sockets that have joined it, so that a
datagram sent to the group's address and a port can reach each of them that is bound to that
port. [`joinMulticast`](#joinMulticast) and [`leaveMulticast`](#leaveMulticast) manage a
socket's membership.

Failures are [`Socket.Error`](Socket#Error) values, whose
[`Socket.ErrorKind`](Socket#ErrorKind) says what went wrong. On native Windows, UDP is not
supported: `bind` fails with [`Socket.NotSupported`](Socket#ErrorKind), and an `onMessage`
subscription is a fatal error.


## Sockets

@docs Socket, Datagram, BindOptions, defaultBindOptions, bind, localEndpoint, close


## Sending and receiving

@docs send, receive, onMessage


## Multicast

@docs joinMulticast, leaveMulticast

aliases.name: BindOptions
aliases.comment:
The settings a socket is bound with.

`address` and `port_` are the local endpoint. Port 0 asks the operating system to choose a free
port, which [`localEndpoint`](#localEndpoint) then reports. The unspecified address
([`Socket.Address.any`](Socket-Address#any)) receives on every interface.

`reuseAddress` lets several sockets that all set it bind the same address and port
(`SO_REUSEADDR`), for example several receivers of one multicast group on one machine.

`broadcast` allows sending to a broadcast address (`SO_BROADCAST`). Without it the operating
system refuses such a send, with [`Socket.PermissionDenied`](Socket#ErrorKind) on Linux.

`ipv6Only` matters only for an IPv6 address. When it is `False`, a socket bound to the
unspecified IPv6 address also exchanges datagrams with IPv4 endpoints, which it sees as
IPv4-mapped addresses. When it is `True`, the socket uses IPv6 only.
aliases.type: { address : Socket.Address.Address, port_ : Basics.Int, reuseAddress : Basics.Bool, broadcast : Basics.Bool, ipv6Only : Basics.Bool }

aliases.name: Datagram
aliases.comment:
A received datagram: its bytes, and the endpoint of the socket that sent it.

On a socket bound to an IPv6 address with `ipv6Only = False`, a datagram from an IPv4 sender
reports the sender as an IPv4-mapped address; [`Socket.Address.unmapIPv4`](Socket-Address#unmapIPv4)
gives the IPv4 address. The sender's address is read from text the kernel prints, and text that
[`Socket.Address.fromString`](Socket-Address#fromString) cannot read becomes the unspecified
address. That can happen for an IPv6 sender whose scope names an interface with a character
other than an ASCII letter or digit, `_`, `.` or `-` in its name.
aliases.type: { data : Bytes.Bytes, from : Socket.Address.InetEndpoint }

aliases.name: Socket
aliases.comment:
A UDP socket bound to a local address and port, made by [`bind`](#bind).

The socket stays open until it is closed with [`close`](#close). On a closed socket, `send`, `receive`, `joinMulticast` and `leaveMulticast`
fail with [`Socket.Cancelled`](Socket#ErrorKind), and `close` does nothing.
aliases.type: Socket.Internal.UdpSocket

values.name: bind
values.comment:
Creates a UDP socket bound to the address and port the options name.

Fails, for example, with [`Socket.AddressInUse`](Socket#ErrorKind) when another socket already
has that address and port, or with [`Socket.AddressNotAvailable`](Socket#ErrorKind) for an
address that does not belong to this machine.

values.name: close
values.comment:
Closes the socket.

Waiting [`receive`](#receive) tasks, and sends still waiting to go out, fail with
[`Socket.Cancelled`](Socket#ErrorKind),
and held datagrams are dropped. Closing a socket that is already closed does nothing.

values.name: defaultBindOptions
values.comment:
Returns the options for binding to `address` and `port_` with `reuseAddress`, `broadcast`
and `ipv6Only` all `False`.

values.name: joinMulticast
values.comment:
Joins a multicast group on one network interface, or with `Nothing` on one the operating
system chooses, so that the socket can receive the datagrams sent to the group at the port it is
bound to.

The interface is given as an address of the group's family; one of the other family fails with
[`Socket.InvalidInput`](Socket#ErrorKind). For IPv4 it is an address of the interface. For IPv6 it is the address's scope that
names the interface, by name or by index, and the address bits are ignored, so `"::%lo"` names
the interface `lo`. With `Nothing`, an IPv6 group's own scope, if it has one, names the
interface instead. An IPv6 interface address with no scope leaves the choice to the operating
system, and the group's own scope is then not used.
values.type: Socket.Address.Address -> Maybe.Maybe Socket.Address.Address -> Socket.Udp.Socket -> Task.Task Socket.Error ()

values.name: leaveMulticast
values.comment:
Leaves a multicast group joined with [`joinMulticast`](#joinMulticast), given the same group
and interface.
values.type: Socket.Address.Address -> Maybe.Maybe Socket.Address.Address -> Socket.Udp.Socket -> Task.Task Socket.Error ()

values.name: localEndpoint
values.comment:
Returns the address and port the socket is bound to, read when the socket was bound. For a
socket bound to port 0, the port is the one the operating system chose. An address
[`Socket.Address.fromString`](Socket-Address#fromString) cannot read, which can happen for an
IPv6 address whose scope names an interface with a character other than an ASCII letter or
digit, `_`, `.` or `-` in its name, is reported as the unspecified address.

values.name: onMessage
values.comment:
Creates a subscription to the datagrams the socket receives that no waiting
[`receive`](#receive) takes, including those held before the subscription started.

    subscriptions : Model -> Sub Msg
    subscriptions model =
        Socket.Udp.onMessage model.socket GotDatagram

A subscription made to a socket that is already closed never fires.

values.name: receive
values.comment:
Waits for the socket's next datagram.

A held datagram, the oldest first, is returned at once. Otherwise the task waits, and a new
datagram goes to the oldest waiting `receive` before any [`onMessage`](#onMessage) subscription
sees it.

Fails with [`Socket.Cancelled`](Socket#ErrorKind) when the socket is closed while the task
waits, and at once on a socket that is already closed.

values.name: send
values.comment:
Sends one datagram holding `data` to the endpoint `to`.

The task succeeds once the operating system has accepted the datagram, which does not mean that
it arrived.

An IPv6 destination on an IPv4 socket fails with
[`Socket.AddressNotAvailable`](Socket#ErrorKind). An IPv4 destination on an IPv6 socket is sent
to its IPv4-mapped address, which works only when the socket was bound with `ipv6Only = False`;
otherwise the send fails with the operating system's error. A datagram too large for the
operating system to send fails, usually with [`Socket.MessageTooLarge`](Socket#ErrorKind); over
IPv4 no datagram can carry more than 65 507 bytes.

name: Socket.Unix
comment:
Programs on the same machine can connect to each other through a name in the file system
instead of a network address, and this module makes such connections and listeners.

A _Unix domain socket_ is a stream socket whose address is a path. A listener creates a _socket
file_ at the path, and a client connects by naming that path. The
[`Connection`](Socket#Connection) and [`Listener`](Socket#Listener) made here are the same types
as for TCP, and are used through [`Socket`](Socket); what is particular to this module is
making them and reading a connection's peer credentials.

A path is handed to the operating system as [`Path.toPosixString`](Path#toPosixString) prints
it. That text must be at most 107 bytes of UTF-8 on Linux and 103 on macOS. On the native backend
under Windows, connecting and listening fail with [`Socket.NotSupported`](Socket#ErrorKind).

Since the address is a path, connecting and listening fail the way a file operation on that path
would: with [`Socket.AddressPathFailed`](Socket#ErrorKind) and the
[`FileSystem.ErrorKind`](FileSystem#ErrorKind) the path would have there, such as
`NoSuchFileOrDirectory`, `NotADirectory`, `LinkLoop`, `ReadOnlyFileSystem`, `PathTooLong` (a
path over the length limit) or `PermissionDenied`. The failures that describe the socket rather
than the path keep their own kinds: [`Socket.AddressInUse`](Socket#ErrorKind) when something
already exists at the path, and [`Socket.ConnectionRefused`](Socket#ErrorKind) when nobody
listens on it.

The socket file's path is the only name a connection has. On the side that connected it is the
remote endpoint, and on the side that accepted it is the local endpoint, in both cases as the path
[`Path.toPosixString`](Path#toPosixString) prints, parsed again; the other endpoint is the empty
path, [`Path.empty`](Path#empty).

A Unix domain connection can also tell who is at the other end: its _peer credentials_ are the
process id, user id and group id of the program on the other side, which
[`peerCredentials`](#peerCredentials) reads.


## Connecting

@docs connect


## Listening

@docs ListenOptions, defaultListenOptions, listen


## Peer credentials

@docs peerCredentials

aliases.name: ListenOptions
aliases.comment:
The options for [`listen`](#listen): where to create the socket file, whether a socket file
already there may be replaced, and the mode to give it.

`removeExisting` removes a socket file already at `path` before listening, whether or not a
program still listens on it. Any other kind of file there, a symbolic link included, still makes
`listen` fail with [`Socket.AddressInUse`](Socket#ErrorKind).

`permissions` is the socket file's mode as a number (`0o600` is `384`), of which only the
low twelve bits, `0o7777`, are used. On the native backend it is set before the socket starts
listening, so no client connects before it applies; on the JavaScript backend it is set once
listening has started, before the task succeeds. `Nothing`, or a negative number, leaves the mode
the process's umask gives. If the mode cannot be set, `listen` fails.
aliases.type: { path : Path.Path, removeExisting : Basics.Bool, permissions : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int }

values.name: connect
values.comment:
Connects to the listener whose socket file is at `path`.

Fails with:

  - [`Socket.AddressPathFailed`](Socket#ErrorKind) `FileSystem.NoSuchFileOrDirectory` when
    nothing exists at the path, and `AddressPathFailed` with another
    [`FileSystem.ErrorKind`](FileSystem#ErrorKind) when the path cannot be used, for example
    `PermissionDenied` without write permission on the socket file, `NotADirectory` when a part
    of the path is not a directory, or `PathTooLong`;
  - [`Socket.ConnectionRefused`](Socket#ErrorKind) when nobody listens on it;
  - on Linux, [`Socket.ListenQueueFull`](Socket#ErrorKind) when the operating system's queue of
    connections waiting on that listener is full.

The connection's remote endpoint is `path`, printed and parsed again, and its local endpoint is
the empty path.

values.name: defaultListenOptions
values.comment:
Returns the options for listening at `path` with which `listen` fails when anything already
exists there, and which leave the socket file's mode to the umask.

values.name: listen
values.comment:
Starts listening at `options.path`, creating the socket file there.

Fails with:

  - [`Socket.AddressInUse`](Socket#ErrorKind) when something already exists at the path and
    `removeExisting` does not allow it to be removed;
  - [`Socket.AddressPathFailed`](Socket#ErrorKind) when the path cannot be used, with the
    [`FileSystem.ErrorKind`](FileSystem#ErrorKind) it would have there: for example
    `NoSuchFileOrDirectory` when a parent directory does not exist, `NotADirectory` when a part
    of the path is not a directory, `PermissionDenied` without write permission on the
    directory, `ReadOnlyFileSystem`, or `PathTooLong`.

A `listen` that fails after creating the socket file removes it again, and so does
[`Socket.closeListener`](Socket#closeListener).

Each connection the listener hands out has as its local endpoint the path printed and parsed
again, and the empty path as its remote endpoint.

values.name: peerCredentials
values.comment:
Asks for the peer credentials of a Unix domain connection: the process id, user id and group
id of the program at the other end, as the operating system reported them when the connection was
made.

Fails with [`Socket.InvalidInput`](Socket#ErrorKind) for a connection that is not a Unix domain
connection, and on the JavaScript backend for one that has closed. Otherwise it fails with
[`Socket.NotSupported`](Socket#ErrorKind) where the credentials cannot be read: on the JavaScript backend for every Unix domain connection, and on the native backend on
systems other than Linux and macOS.
values.type: Socket.Connection -> Task.Task Socket.Error { pid : Basics.Int, uid : Basics.Int, gid : Basics.Int }

name: Stream
comment:
Everything in this package that moves data over time, such as standard input and output, a
file read or written in pieces, a child program's pipes, a network connection, an HTTP body or a
WebSocket message, is handed to the program as a stream. This module is what can be done with
one: read from it, write to it, end it, and connect streams together.

A stream has two sides. Values go into its _writable_ side and come out of its _readable_ side,
in the order they went in, unless a transformation changes them on the way. The program holds a
handle to a side: a [`Readable`](#Readable) to read from, or a [`Writable`](#Writable) to write
into. A stream made by [`fromList`](#fromList) or by
[`Stream.Transformation`](Stream-Transformation) lives in memory. A stream that another module
creates over a file, pipe or socket is handed out as one side only, and the resource is on the
other side.

Each side of an in-memory stream buffers a limited number of values, so a writer cannot run
arbitrarily far ahead of its reader. This is _backpressure_, and it is why there are two ways
to write. [`write`](#write) succeeds once the value has been _accepted_: taken from the
writable side's buffer and passed on to the readable side (through the transformation, if there
is one), or, for a stream over a resource, written to it. [`enqueue`](#enqueue) succeeds
as soon as the value is in the writable side's buffer. On an in-memory stream both wait while
that buffer is full.

A stream ends in one of three ways, and they are reported differently.

  - It is _closed_ when its writer says no more values will come
    ([`closeWritable`](#closeWritable)), or when the resource behind it has no more to give: the
    values already written can still be read, and after the last of them a read fails with
    `Closed`. A write or a close into a closed stream fails with `Closed` too.
  - It is _cancelled_ when the program gives up on it, with a reason:
    [`cancelReadable`](#cancelReadable), [`cancelWritable`](#cancelWritable), or a custom
    transformation whose step returns `Cancel`. Buffered values are dropped, except the bytes
    [`readLine`](#readLine) has kept, and reads, writes and closes fail with `Cancelled` and the
    reason, except reads after [`cancelReadable`](#cancelReadable), which fail as
    [`cancelReadable`](#cancelReadable) describes.
  - It has _failed_ when the resource behind it fails, such as a connection the peer reset or a
    file that cannot be read. Buffered values are dropped as for a cancel, and reads, writes and
    closes fail with `Failed` and a [`Failure`](#Failure).

Once a stream has been handed out, a failure is how a problem with its resource reaches the
program. A connection reset, for example, is a read that fails with `Failed`, not an error of the
module that made the connection; [`Socket.fromStreamFailure`](Socket#fromStreamFailure) reads
that failure back as a [`Socket.Error`](Socket#Error).

A side is _locked_ while an operation holds it, such as a read waiting for a value, a write
waiting for room in the buffer, or a pipe ([`pipeThrough`](#pipeThrough), [`pipeTo`](#pipeTo)),
which holds the readable side of its source and the writable side of its destination until it
finishes. Another operation that needs a locked side fails at once with `Locked`.

[`readLine`](#readLine) reads a byte stream a line at a time. The bytes it reads past the end
of a line are kept with the stream, and the next [`read`](#read), [`readString`](#readString),
[`readLine`](#readLine) or [`readUntilClosed`](#readUntilClosed) hands them out first, so line
reads and chunk reads can be mixed. A pipe does not hand them out: bytes kept by `readLine` are
not moved by [`pipeThrough`](#pipeThrough) or [`pipeTo`](#pipeTo). At the end of a stream they
can be lost, as [`readLine`](#readLine) describes.


# Readable Streams

@docs Readable, fromList, read, readString, readLine, readUntilClosed, cancelReadable


# Writable Streams

@docs Writable, write, writeString, writeLine, enqueue, closeWritable, cancelWritable


# Logging

The logging functions write to a byte stream and ignore any failure. They are for output where
there is nothing sensible to do when a write fails: if an error message cannot be written to
the terminal, there is usually nowhere else to report that either.

@docs log, logString, logLine


# Error Handling

`Stream` knows only what any stream can go through. Why the resource behind a stream failed is
known to the module that made the stream, and each such module reads a [`Failure`](#Failure)
back as its own error type, as [`Failure`](#Failure) describes.

@docs Error, errorToString, Failure, failureToString


# Transformation Streams

@docs Transformation, pipeThrough, awaitAndPipeThrough, pipeTo

unions.name: Error
unions.comment:
Why an operation on a stream failed.

`Closed` means that the stream has ended. A read gets it when the stream has ended normally: it
was closed, and every value written before the close has been read. A read also gets `Closed`
after the stream was cancelled from its reading side with [`cancelReadable`](#cancelReadable),
unless it had already been cancelled or failed in another way. A write or a close gets `Closed`
when the stream has been closed, or when its transformation has ended it, as a custom
transformation's `Close` does.

`Cancelled` means that the program cancelled the stream, and carries the reason it gave, a
human-readable explanation: the reason given to [`cancelReadable`](#cancelReadable) or
[`cancelWritable`](#cancelWritable), to a custom transformation's `Cancel`, or returned as the
`Err` of a [`readUntilClosed`](#readUntilClosed) step. [`readString`](#readString) and
[`readLine`](#readLine) cancel a stream themselves, with a reason of their own, when the bytes
are not valid UTF-8. A read gets `Cancelled` when the stream was cancelled from its writing side
or by its transformation; a write or a close gets it when the stream has been cancelled; and
[`pipeTo`](#pipeTo) gets it as [`pipeTo`](#pipeTo) describes.

`Failed` means that the resource behind the stream failed, for example a connection the peer
reset, and carries a [`Failure`](#Failure) describing it.

`Locked` means that the side of the stream the operation needs is held by another operation,
such as a waiting read, a write waiting for room, or a pipe. A single read, write, close, cancel
or pipe that fails with `Locked` has done nothing and can be tried again once the other has
finished; a function that reads and then cancels or reads again, such as
[`readString`](#readString), [`readLine`](#readLine) or [`readUntilClosed`](#readUntilClosed), may
already have consumed values.

aliases.name: Failure
aliases.comment:
Why the resource behind a stream failed: a stream over a file, a pipe, a connection or an
HTTP body that could not go on.

A `Failure` is opaque, because `Stream` knows nothing about the resources behind streams. The
module that made the stream knows, and reads its own failures back as its own error type, giving
`Nothing` for a failure some other module made:

  - [`Socket.fromStreamFailure`](Socket#fromStreamFailure), for the streams of a TCP or Unix
    domain connection, gives a [`Socket.Error`](Socket#Error), such as one whose kind is
    `ConnectionReset`;
  - [`Socket.Tls.fromStreamFailure`](Socket-Tls#fromStreamFailure), for the streams of a TLS
    connection, gives a [`Socket.Tls.Error`](Socket-Tls#Error), covering both TLS failures and
    failures of the connection under it;
  - [`FileSystem.fromStreamFailure`](FileSystem#fromStreamFailure), for file streams, gives a
    [`FileSystem.Error`](FileSystem#Error);
  - [`WebSocket.fromStreamFailure`](WebSocket#fromStreamFailure), for a WebSocket's message
    streams, gives a [`WebSocket.Error`](WebSocket#Error);
  - [`Http.Stream.fromStreamFailure`](Http-Stream#fromStreamFailure), for streaming HTTP bodies,
    gives an `Http.Error`.

The failures of a child process's pipes, and of a decompressing transformation, have no such
module: [`failureToString`](#failureToString) describes them.

Only the streams this package makes over a resource fail with a `Failure`. A stream made in Elm,
such as a custom transformation, ends with `Closed` or is cancelled with a reason.
aliases.type: Stream.Internal.Failure

aliases.name: Readable
aliases.comment:
The readable side of a stream, from which values of type `value` are read. One is made by
[`fromList`](#fromList) or [`pipeThrough`](#pipeThrough), taken from a transformation with
[`Stream.Transformation.readable`](Stream-Transformation#readable), or handed out by another
module of this package.
aliases.type: Stream.Internal.Readable value

aliases.name: Transformation
aliases.comment:
An in-memory stream whose two sides are both in the program's hands, and which may change
the values on their way through: it can alter them, drop them, or produce several from one.

A `Transformation input output` accepts `input` values on its
[`writable`](Stream-Transformation#writable) side and produces `output` values on its
[`readable`](Stream-Transformation#readable) side;
[`textEncoder`](Stream-Transformation#textEncoder), for example, makes a
`Transformation String Bytes`.

Transformations are created with the functions in
[`Stream.Transformation`](Stream-Transformation), and used with [`pipeThrough`](#pipeThrough).
aliases.type: Stream.Internal.Transformation input output

aliases.name: Writable
aliases.comment:
The writable side of a stream, into which values of type `value` are written. One is taken
from a transformation with [`Stream.Transformation.writable`](Stream-Transformation#writable), or
handed out by another module of this package.
aliases.type: Stream.Internal.Writable value

values.name: awaitAndPipeThrough
values.comment:
Waits for the `Task` that builds a [`Transformation`](#Transformation), such as
[`Stream.Transformation.gunzip`](Stream-Transformation#gunzip), then pipes the `Readable` through
it as [`pipeThrough`](#pipeThrough) does. A failure of the building `Task` fails this one.
values.type: Task.Task Stream.Error (Stream.Transformation input output) -> Stream.Readable input -> Task.Task Stream.Error (Stream.Readable output)

values.name: cancelReadable
values.comment:
Cancels the stream from its reading side, because the reader will not take any more values.
The `String` is the reason, a human-readable explanation of what went wrong. Values in the
stream's buffer are dropped, except the bytes [`readLine`](#readLine) has kept, and a stream over
a resource stops reading from it.

Once any kept bytes have been handed out, later reads fail with `Closed`, unless the stream had
already been cancelled from its writing side or by its transformation, in which case they go on
failing with `Cancelled` and that earlier reason, or its resource had failed, in which case they
go on failing with `Failed` and that failure. If the writing side is still open, or a close of it is still in progress, writes into it
that are still waiting, that close, and later writes fail with `Cancelled` and the given reason.
While a read is waiting on the stream, or something else such as a pipe is consuming it, the
`Task` fails with `Locked` and nothing is cancelled.

values.name: cancelWritable
values.comment:
Cancels the stream from its writing side, because something has gone wrong. The `String` is
the reason, a human-readable explanation of what. Values in the stream's buffers are dropped,
except the bytes [`readLine`](#readLine) has kept.

On an in-memory stream, writes still in the buffer and a close still in progress fail with
`Cancelled` and the given reason, and so do reads from the readable side, including one already
waiting, once any kept bytes have been handed out. A stream over a resource stops writing to it.
Cancelling a stream that is already closed or cancelled does nothing. While a write is waiting
for room, or a pipe is writing into the stream, the `Task` fails with `Locked` and nothing is
cancelled.

values.name: closeWritable
values.comment:
Closes the stream: no more values will be written into it. The `Task` succeeds once every
value written before the close has been accepted, and, for a stream over a resource, once the
resource has been closed (the standard streams are never closed; the close only waits for their
writes). Readers can still read the values in the buffer, and then get `Closed`.

Closing a stream that is already closed or being closed fails with `Closed`, and one that has
been cancelled or has failed fails with `Cancelled` and the reason, or `Failed` and the failure.
While a write is waiting for room, or a pipe is writing into the stream, it fails with `Locked`.
If the stream is cancelled while the close waits, the `Task` fails with `Cancelled` and the
reason, and if its resource fails, with `Failed` and the failure.

values.name: enqueue
values.comment:
Queues a value to be written into the stream, and succeeds once it is in the writable side's
buffer, or, for a stream over a resource, once the write has been started.

The difference from [`write`](#write) is when the `Task` succeeds. It does not wait for a reader
to take the value, so it succeeds even if nothing is reading, as long as the buffer has room (on
an in-memory stream with a full buffer it waits for room). The price is that it cannot report
what happens to the value afterwards: if the stream is cancelled, or the write to the resource
fails, before the value is accepted, this `Task` has already succeeded.

Enqueueing into a stream that has been closed, cancelled or has failed fails as
[`write`](#write) does, and it fails with `Locked` in the same cases as [`write`](#write).
values.type: value -> Stream.Writable value -> Task.Task Stream.Error (Stream.Writable value)

values.name: errorToString
values.comment:
Returns a human-readable description of an error: `"Closed"`, `"Locked"`, `"Cancelled: "`
followed by the reason, or `"Failed: "` followed by
[`failureToString`](#failureToString) of the failure.

values.name: failureToString
values.comment:
Returns a human-readable description of a failure, naming the problem, for example
`"read ECONNRESET"` for a connection the peer reset.

values.name: fromList
values.comment:
Creates an in-memory [`Readable`](#Readable) stream that delivers the values in the given
`List`, in order, and is then closed.

The stream's buffer is made large enough for the whole list, so the `Task` does not wait for a
reader.

values.name: log
values.comment:
Writes `Bytes` into a byte stream as [`write`](#write) does, and succeeds once the write has
succeeded or failed, ignoring any failure.

values.name: logLine
values.comment:
Writes a `String` followed by a newline into a byte stream as [`writeLine`](#writeLine)
does, ignoring any failure.

    Stream.logLine "Hello, world!" env.stdout

values.name: logString
values.comment:
Writes a `String` into a byte stream as [`writeString`](#writeString) does, ignoring any
failure.

values.name: pipeThrough
values.comment:
Starts moving every value of the `Readable` into the writable side of the
[`Transformation`](#Transformation), and succeeds at once with the transformation's readable
side.

The pipe locks the source and the transformation's writable side until it finishes. When the
source has closed and every value has been moved, the transformation's writable side is closed.
If the source is cancelled from its writing side, the transformation is cancelled with the same
reason, so reads from the result fail with `Cancelled`; if its resource fails, the
transformation ends with the same failure, so reads from the result fail with `Failed`. If the
transformation's writable side is cancelled, for example by cancelling the result, the source
is cancelled with the same reason. These later failures are not reported by this `Task`, which
has already succeeded.

If the source or the transformation's writable side is already locked, the `Task` fails with
`Locked`.
values.type: Stream.Transformation input output -> Stream.Readable input -> Task.Task Stream.Error (Stream.Readable output)

values.name: pipeTo
values.comment:
Moves every value of the `Readable` into the `Writable`, locking both until it finishes.

When the readable side has closed and every value has been moved, the writable side is closed,
and the `Task` succeeds once that close has finished.

If the readable side is cancelled from its writing side, the writable side is cancelled with the
same reason, and the `Task` fails with `Cancelled` and that reason. If the readable side's
resource fails, the writable side ends with the same failure, and the `Task` fails with `Failed`
and that failure.

If the writable side is cancelled (by its reader or by its transformation) or its resource fails,
or it is already closed or being closed when the pipe starts, the readable side is cancelled from
its reading side, and the `Task` fails with the writable side's error: `Cancelled` and the
reason, `Failed` and the failure, or `Closed` for a closed one.

If either side is already locked, the `Task` fails with `Locked`.
values.type: Stream.Writable data -> Stream.Readable data -> Task.Task Stream.Error ()

values.name: read
values.comment:
Reads the next value off the stream, waiting until there is one.

Once the stream has been closed and every value written before the close has been read, or
once the reading side has been cancelled while the stream had not been cancelled or failed in
another way, the `Task` fails with `Closed`. If the stream has been cancelled from its writing
side or by its transformation, it fails with `Cancelled` and the reason, and if its resource has
failed, with `Failed` and the failure. While another read is waiting on the stream, or something
else such as a pipe is consuming it, it fails with `Locked`.

Killing a task whose read is waiting (`Process.kill`) withdraws the read: the stream is no
longer locked, the wait no longer keeps the program running, and no input is lost, since a
value that arrives for the withdrawn read is kept for the next one.

values.name: readLine
values.comment:
Reads the next line off a byte stream: everything up to the next newline (`\n`), decoded as
UTF-8, without the newline and without a carriage return (`\r`) just before it.

    countLines : Readable Bytes -> Int -> Task Error Int
    countLines stdin n =
        Stream.readLine stdin
            |> Task.andThen (\_ -> countLines stdin (n + 1))
            |> Task.onError
                (\err ->
                    case err of
                        Stream.Closed ->
                            Task.succeed n

                        _ ->
                            Task.fail err
                )

A line may be longer than the chunks the stream delivers. On the standard input stream, once it
has been closed, a last line without a newline is returned as it is, and after that the `Task`
fails with `Closed`. On other streams this is not guaranteed: when such a stream ends, the bytes
`readLine` has kept can be lost, including whole lines of the last chunk of an in-memory stream.
Bytes read past the newline are kept with the stream and handed out first by the next read, so
`readLine` can be mixed with [`read`](#read) and [`readString`](#readString). If a line is not
valid UTF-8, the stream is cancelled, with a reason saying so, and the `Task` fails with
`Cancelled`, or with `Locked` if by
then another operation holds the reading side. A cancel does not drop the kept bytes: after
one, the next `read` still hands them out before it fails, and `readLine` still returns any
complete lines among them. Other failures are those of [`read`](#read).

values.name: readString
values.comment:
Reads the next chunk of `Bytes` off the stream, as [`read`](#read) does, and converts it to
a `String`. If the chunk is not valid UTF-8, the stream is cancelled, with a reason saying so,
and the `Task` fails with `Cancelled`; if by then another operation holds the reading side, the `Task` fails with `Locked`
instead and the stream is not cancelled.

Each chunk is converted on its own, so a multi-byte character split across two chunks does not
convert. [`readLine`](#readLine) assembles lines across chunks, and
[`Stream.Transformation.textDecoder`](Stream-Transformation#textDecoder) decodes a whole byte
stream however it is split.

values.name: readUntilClosed
values.comment:
Reads every value off the stream, folding each into an accumulated value with `stepFn`,
starting from `initial`, and succeeds with the result once a read fails with `Closed`.

If `stepFn` returns an `Err`, its `String` is used as the reason to cancel the stream, and the
`Task` fails with `Cancelled` and that reason; if by then another operation holds the reading
side, the `Task` fails with `Locked` instead and the stream is not cancelled. Any other failure of
a read fails the `Task`.
values.type: (a -> b -> Result.Result String.String b) -> b -> Stream.Readable a -> Task.Task Stream.Error b

values.name: write
values.comment:
Writes a value into the stream, and succeeds once the value has been accepted: passed on
to the stream's readable side (through the transformation, if there is one), or, for a stream
over a resource, written to it. On an in-memory stream with no room for the value, this waits
until a reader makes room.

Writing into a stream that has been closed fails with `Closed`, into one that has been
cancelled with `Cancelled` and the reason, and into one whose resource has failed with `Failed`
and the failure. While another write is waiting for room, or a pipe is writing into the stream,
it fails with `Locked`.
values.type: value -> Stream.Writable value -> Task.Task Stream.Error (Stream.Writable value)

values.name: writeLine
values.comment:
Appends a newline (`\n`) to the `String`, converts it to UTF-8 `Bytes` and writes them into
the stream, as [`write`](#write) does. A lone surrogate is converted as
[`writeString`](#writeString) describes.
values.type: String.String -> Stream.Writable Bytes.Bytes -> Task.Task Stream.Error (Stream.Writable Bytes.Bytes)

values.name: writeString
values.comment:
Converts the `String` to UTF-8 `Bytes` and writes them into the stream, as
[`write`](#write) does.

A lone surrogate (half of a UTF-16 pair with no partner) is converted differently by the two
backends: the JavaScript backend writes U+FFFD in its place, and the native backend writes the
surrogate's own three bytes, which are not valid UTF-8 and which [`readString`](#readString)
rejects.
values.type: String.String -> Stream.Writable Bytes.Bytes -> Task.Task Stream.Error (Stream.Writable Bytes.Bytes)

name: Stream.Transformation
comment:
A [`Transformation`](Stream#Transformation) is an in-memory stream that changes the values
passing through it, and this module is where transformations are made: ones that pass values on
unchanged, ones driven by an Elm function, and built-in ones for text and compression.

    Stream.Transformation.gunzip
        |> Task.andThen (\gunzip -> Stream.pipeThrough gunzip compressed)

Everything here that makes a transformation is a `Task`, not a `Transformation`. Each run of the
task creates a new transformation with nothing in it. [`readable`](#readable) and
[`writable`](#writable) give its two sides: values written into the writable side come out,
transformed, on the readable side. Reading, writing, closing, cancelling and piping work on those
sides as [`Stream`](Stream) describes.

Each side has a _capacity_, a number of values. The writable side holds up to its capacity of
values written but not yet transformed, and the readable side holds results not yet read. A value
is transformed as it leaves the writable side, which happens only while the readable side holds
fewer results than its capacity (or, at a read capacity of 0, while a reader waits; see
[`customWith`](#customWith)), so a reader that falls behind fills the readable side first, then
the writable side, after which a write waits for room, as [`Stream.write`](Stream#write)
describes. A [`Stream.write`](Stream#write) into a transformation succeeds once its value has
been transformed, not once the results have been read.

A transformation can end early in two ways, and both act on both sides: results not yet read
are dropped, and writes still waiting, later writes, a close and later reads fail, apart from
bytes [`Stream.readLine`](Stream#readLine) has kept, which can still be read.

  - A custom transformation whose step returns `Cancel` is cancelled, and these fail with
    `Stream.Cancelled` and the step's reason.
  - A decompressor that cannot go on has failed, as each decompressor describes, and these fail
    with `Stream.Failed` and a [`Stream.Failure`](Stream#Failure) describing the problem, which
    [`Stream.failureToString`](Stream#failureToString) reads.


# Building Transformations

An _identity_ transformation passes every value on unchanged. A _custom_ transformation calls an
Elm function, its _step_, for each value written, with a state the step carries from one value to
the next; [`CustomAction`](#CustomAction) is what a step returns.

@docs identity, identityWith, null, CustomAction, custom, customWith


# Using Transformations

@docs readable, writable


# Text

The text transformations convert between `String` and UTF-8 `Bytes`, and never fail. Neither
produces an empty value: an input that yields nothing yet, such as an empty string, produces no
output. Each side has a capacity of one value.

@docs textEncoder, textDecoder


# Compression

Six transformations from `Bytes` to `Bytes`, using zlib, in three formats: gzip, deflate data in
the zlib format, which adds a header and a checksum, and raw deflate data, which has neither. Each
side has a capacity of one value, but one value written can produce several outputs. Each output is
at most 64 KiB.

A compressor does not produce output for every value written: zlib holds data back until it has
enough to emit, and writes the rest when the writable side is closed, so a reader may get nothing
until then.

A decompressor that fails ends the transformation with a `Stream.Failed` failure describing the
problem, as described above. A `write` of the value that carried the bad data fails, and a close
fails when the compressed data was incomplete.

@docs gzip, gunzip, deflate, inflate, deflateRaw, inflateRaw

unions.name: CustomAction
unions.comment:
What a custom transformation's step does with one value written into it: carry on with a new
state, possibly producing values, or end the transformation.

`UpdateState` carries the new state and produces nothing.

`Send` carries the new state and the values to make readable, in order. All of them are put in
the readable side's buffer, even beyond its capacity; no further value is transformed until
readers have brought the buffer back below its capacity, or, at a read capacity of 0, emptied it
and wait for more.

`Close` ends the transformation after the values it carries. They are made readable, and once
they and the values before them have been read, reads fail with `Stream.Closed`. Writes still
waiting to be transformed, a close in progress, and every later write or close fail with
`Stream.Closed` too.

`Cancel` cancels the transformation on both sides with the given reason, so that reads, writes
and closes fail with `Stream.Cancelled` and that reason, as the module documentation describes.

With `Close` and `Cancel`, the write of the value that produced them still succeeds.

values.name: custom
values.comment:
Creates a custom transformation. For each value written, in order, the step is called with the
current state and the value, and the [`CustomAction`](#CustomAction) it returns says what happens.
The second argument is the first state. Each side has a capacity of one value.

The step is called only for values written. Closing the writable side does not call it, so
anything the step holds in its state, such as a partial batch, is not produced at the close; the
readable side closes once its buffered values have been read.
values.type: (state -> input -> Stream.Transformation.CustomAction state output) -> state -> Task.Task x (Stream.Transformation input output)

values.name: customWith
values.comment:
Creates a custom transformation, as [`custom`](#custom) does, with the given first state and
capacities.

A write capacity below 1 is raised to 1, and a read capacity below 0 to 0. With a read capacity of
0, a value is transformed only when nothing is buffered on the readable side and a read is waiting
on it, or a pipe out of it is ready for a value.
values.type: (state -> input -> Stream.Transformation.CustomAction state output) -> { initialState : state, readCapacity : Basics.Int, writeCapacity : Basics.Int } -> Task.Task x (Stream.Transformation input output)

values.name: deflate
values.comment:
A task that creates a transformation that compresses `Bytes` into deflate data in the zlib
format.

values.name: deflateRaw
values.comment:
A task that creates a transformation that compresses `Bytes` into raw deflate data, with no
header or checksum.

values.name: gunzip
values.comment:
A task that creates a transformation that decompresses gzip-format `Bytes`.

The transformation fails, with `Stream.Failed`, when the data cannot be decompressed, or when
the writable side is closed before the compressed data is complete. Data after the end of the
compressed data is treated differently by the two backends: the native backend fails the
transformation; on the JavaScript backend, whether such data is decompressed, ignored or fails
the transformation depends on the data and on how it was split into written values.

values.name: gzip
values.comment: A task that creates a transformation that compresses `Bytes` into the gzip format.

values.name: identity
values.comment:
A task that creates an identity transformation, whose sides each have a capacity of one value.

Handing its readable side to another part of a program gives that part a one-way channel from
whoever holds the writable side.

values.name: identityWith
values.comment:
Creates an identity transformation, as [`identity`](#identity) does, with the given
capacities. A capacity below 1 is raised to 1.
values.type: { readCapacity : Basics.Int, writeCapacity : Basics.Int } -> Task.Task x (Stream.Transformation data data)

values.name: inflate
values.comment:
A task that creates a transformation that decompresses deflate data in the zlib format.

The transformation fails, with `Stream.Failed`, when the data cannot be decompressed, or when
the writable side is closed before the compressed data is complete. Data after the end of the
compressed data fails it on the native backend, and is ignored on the JavaScript backend.

values.name: inflateRaw
values.comment:
A task that creates a transformation that decompresses raw deflate data, which has no header
or checksum.

The transformation fails, with `Stream.Failed`, when the data cannot be decompressed, or when
the writable side is closed before the compressed data is complete. Data after the end of the
compressed data fails it on the native backend, and is ignored on the JavaScript backend.

values.name: null
values.comment:
Creates a transformation that accepts every value written into it and drops it. Its readable
side never gives a value, and is closed when the writable side is closed.

The argument becomes the step's state, which nothing reads, so any value will do. Each side
has a capacity of one value.

values.name: readable
values.comment: Returns the readable side of a transformation, from which its output values are read.

values.name: textDecoder
values.comment:
A task that creates a transformation from UTF-8 `Bytes` to `String`s.

The bytes may be split anywhere: a character split across two chunks is decoded whole. Invalid
bytes are replaced by the replacement character U+FFFD, rather than failing the transformation,
and so is a character left incomplete when the writable side is closed. A byte order mark at the
very start is removed.

values.name: textEncoder
values.comment:
A task that creates a transformation from `String`s to their UTF-8 encoding as `Bytes`.

A surrogate pair split across two strings is encoded as the one character it stands for. A lone
surrogate becomes U+FFFD, on both backends, unlike [`Stream.writeString`](Stream#writeString).

values.name: writable
values.comment: Returns the writable side of a transformation, into which its input values are written.

name: System
comment:
An Eco system program is an ordinary Elm `Platform.Program` that runs as a command-line tool
or a server, and this module is what makes it one: the [`Environment`](#Environment) it starts
with, and the controls that act on the whole running program, such as its exit code and the
signals sent to it.

The flags of such a program are an `Environment`. Eco recognises a `main` whose flags type is
`System.Environment` and builds the environment itself when the program starts, so any flags
JSON a host supplies is ignored. The environment tells you which platform the program is
running on, which arguments it was started with and when it started, and gives you its standard
input, output and error streams.

A long-running program, one that keeps state, reacts to messages and listens to
subscriptions, is made with [`program`](#program):

    main : Platform.Program System.Environment Model Msg
    main =
        System.program
            { init = \env -> ( initialModel env, Cmd.none )
            , update = update
            , subscriptions = subscriptions
            }

A _simple program_ runs a single task and then ends. It is made with
[`simpleProgram`](#simpleProgram):

    main : Platform.Program System.Environment () ()
    main =
        System.simpleProgram
            (\env -> Stream.logLine "Hello, world!" env.stdout)

A program runs while it is waiting for something it asked for, and ends when it is not. It is
waiting while a task it started has not finished, such as a read, a write, an `accept`, a
sleep, an HTTP request or a child process it spawned; while it subscribes to something that can
still deliver, such as new connections on an open listener, messages on an open WebSocket or
changes to a watched file; and while it owes an answer to an HTTP request it was given.
Opening something does not keep a program running: an open listener with no `accept` waiting
and no subscription, or an open connection with no read or write in progress, does not.
Connections, datagrams and requests that arrive while nothing asks for them are held for later
and do not keep a program running either. Some subscriptions never keep a program running,
because they wait for things the program did not ask for; their docs say so.

When nothing is left to wait for, the program has an _empty event loop_ and ends, unless it
subscribes to [`onEmptyEventLoop`](#onEmptyEventLoop), which is told once and can ask to be
told again with [`rearmEmptyEventLoop`](#rearmEmptyEventLoop). [`exit`](#exit) and
[`exitWithCode`](#exitWithCode) end the program at once, whatever it is waiting for.

The same rule covers the `elm/*` packages. A `Process.sleep` keeps the program running until it
ends, a `Time.every` subscription while it exists, and an `elm/http` request while it is in
flight. `Http.track` adds nothing of its own: a tracker with no request in flight does not keep
the program running.

Eco compiles a program either to native code or to JavaScript run by Node. Where the two
behave differently, the docstrings say so. A native program can also be embedded in a host
application, which then owns the process. An embedded program does not end when it runs out of
work: it runs until the host stops it or it calls [`exitWithCode`](#exitWithCode). Embedding
also changes what exiting and signals do, as the functions below describe.


# Programs

@docs program, simpleProgram


# Environment information

@docs Environment, environmentVariables, Platform, CpuArchitecture


# Exit

@docs exit, exitWithCode, setExitCode


# Subscriptions

@docs onEmptyEventLoop, rearmEmptyEventLoop, onSignalInterrupt, onSignalTerminate

unions.name: CpuArchitecture
unions.comment:
The processor architecture a program is running on, spelled as Node's `process.arch` spells
it. `X64` is 64-bit x86 and `IA32` 32-bit x86; `Arm` and `Arm64` are 32-bit and 64-bit Arm;
`Mips` and `Mipsel` are big-endian and little-endian MIPS; `PPC` and `PPC64` are 32-bit and
64-bit PowerPC; `S390` and `S390x` are 31-bit and 64-bit IBM mainframe (s390) processors.

`UnknownArchitecture` carries the name of any other architecture, as the backend reported it.
On the native backend the architecture is fixed when the program is compiled; 64-bit RISC-V is
reported as `UnknownArchitecture "riscv64"`, and any other architecture this type does not
name as `UnknownArchitecture "unknown"`.

unions.name: Platform
unions.comment:
The operating system a program is running on, spelled as Node's `process.platform` spells
it. `Win32` is Windows and `Darwin` is macOS; `Linux`, `FreeBSD`, `OpenBSD`, `SunOS` and
`Aix` are the systems they name.

`UnknownPlatform` carries the name of any other platform, as the backend reported it. On the
native backend the platform is fixed when the program is compiled, and one this type does not
name is reported as `UnknownPlatform "unknown"`.

aliases.name: Environment
aliases.comment:
What a program is told about itself when it starts: the platform it runs on, how it was
started, and its standard streams.

  - `applicationPath` is the path of the running program. On the native backend it is the
    executable, with symbolic links resolved where the system allows it, or `Path.empty` where
    it cannot be read, which includes every system other than Linux and macOS. On the
    JavaScript backend it is the path of the compiled JavaScript file, with symbolic links
    resolved where possible, or of the `node` executable when the program is not loaded as a
    CommonJS module. The text is read with [`Path.fromPosixString`](Path#fromPosixString) on every
    system.
  - `args` holds the command line arguments. On the native backend, on Linux, macOS and
    Windows, it is the process's C `argv`, so it starts with the program as it was invoked;
    elsewhere the list is empty. Embedded
    in a host application, it is the host's `argv`. On the JavaScript backend it is Node's
    `process.argv` without the `node` executable, so it starts with the script.
  - `startTime` is read once, when the environment is built just before `init`, so `init` does
    not need to ask for the time.
  - `stdout`, `stderr` and `stdin` are three separate streams over the process's standard
    output, error and input; the `Stream` module says what can be done with them, and
    `Stream.readLine` reads standard input a line at a time. Closing or cancelling one of them
    ends that stream but leaves the process's standard file descriptor open.
aliases.type: { platform : System.Platform, cpuArchitecture : System.CpuArchitecture, applicationPath : Path.Path, args : List.List String.String, startTime : Time.Posix, stdout : Stream.Writable Bytes.Bytes, stderr : Stream.Writable Bytes.Bytes, stdin : Stream.Readable Bytes.Bytes }

values.name: environmentVariables
values.comment:
Reads the environment variables of the running process, mapping each variable's name to
its value.

The variables are read when the task runs, not when the program starts. On the native backend
an entry with no `=` is read as a name with the empty value.

values.name: exit
values.comment: Ends the program at once with exit code 0, as `exitWithCode 0` does.

values.name: exitWithCode
values.comment:
Ends the program at once with exit `code`.

It does not wait for work still in progress, such as an HTTP request, a file write, a stream
write that has not yet succeeded, or a value `Stream.enqueue` has queued but not yet written,
so it is for a state where continuing makes no sense; to end once that work is done, use
[`setExitCode`](#setExitCode) instead. The exit code can be read by the process that started
the program.

On the native backend, when the program is embedded in a host application, the process is not
ended: the program stops and the host receives `code`.

values.name: onEmptyEventLoop
values.comment:
Creates a subscription that receives `msg` when the program has an empty event loop:
nothing it is waiting for is left, so the program would otherwise end.

The message arrives once. Work started while handling it runs to completion, and the next time
the event loop is empty the program ends. To receive the message again at the next empty
event loop, issue [`rearmEmptyEventLoop`](#rearmEmptyEventLoop). If the program has several
`onEmptyEventLoop` subscriptions, each receives its message at the same moment.

Whether the message is due is one setting for the whole run of the program. It starts on, so a
program that subscribes some time after it starts still receives the message once. Delivering
the message turns it off, and only `rearmEmptyEventLoop` turns it on again: subscribing anew
after a delivery is not enough.

The subscription does not keep the program running. On the native backend it never fires
when the program is embedded in a host application.

values.name: onSignalInterrupt
values.comment:
Creates a subscription that receives `msg` when the process is sent an interrupt
signal (`SIGINT`, the signal a terminal sends on Ctrl+C).

While the subscription exists, the signal no longer ends the program, so ending it is up to the
program. The subscription does not keep the program running. On the native backend it has no
effect on Windows or when the program is embedded in a host application: it never fires, and
the signal is handled as it would be without it.

values.name: onSignalTerminate
values.comment:
Creates a subscription that receives `msg` when the process is sent a terminate
signal (`SIGTERM`, the request to shut down that service managers and the `kill` command send).

While the subscription exists, the signal no longer ends the program, so ending it is up to the
program. The subscription does not keep the program running. On the native backend it has no
effect on Windows or when the program is embedded in a host application: it never fires, and
the signal is handled as it would be without it.

values.name: program
values.comment:
Creates a long-running program from an `init`, an `update` and `subscriptions`, as
`Platform.worker` does, with the program's [`Environment`](#Environment) as its flags.

The program runs while it is waiting for something, as the module documentation describes,
and ends when it has an empty event loop that [`onEmptyEventLoop`](#onEmptyEventLoop) does not
take over.
values.type: { init : System.Environment -> ( model, Platform.Cmd.Cmd msg ), update : msg -> model -> ( model, Platform.Cmd.Cmd msg ), subscriptions : model -> Platform.Sub.Sub msg } -> Platform.Program System.Environment model msg

values.name: rearmEmptyEventLoop
values.comment:
Asks for [`onEmptyEventLoop`](#onEmptyEventLoop) to deliver its message again the next
time the program has an empty event loop.

Issue it while handling that message, or in any later update before the event loop is next
empty, for example once more jobs have been queued. If the program issues it and then starts
no work, the event loop is empty again at once, so the message arrives again at once; a
program that issues it on every delivery without starting work never ends. Issuing it when
there is no `onEmptyEventLoop` subscription has no effect until the program subscribes.

values.name: setExitCode
values.comment:
Sets the exit code the program ends with, without ending it.

A later `setExitCode` replaces the code, and [`exitWithCode`](#exitWithCode) ends the program
with its own.

values.name: simpleProgram
values.comment:
Creates a simple program: one that runs the task `run` makes from the
[`Environment`](#Environment), and has no state, messages or subscriptions.

The task's result is ignored. If the task fails, the program's exit code is set to 1, as
[`setExitCode`](#setExitCode) sets it; if it succeeds, the exit code is left as it is, which is
0 unless the task set another. The program ends as any program does, so it waits for IO the
task started even after the task has finished. To end with a particular non-zero exit code,
finish the task with [`setExitCode`](#setExitCode):

    main : Platform.Program System.Environment () ()
    main =
        System.simpleProgram
            (\env ->
                case List.drop 1 env.args of
                    [] ->
                        Stream.logLine "usage: greet NAME" env.stderr
                            |> Task.andThen (\_ -> System.setExitCode 2)

                    name :: _ ->
                        Stream.logLine ("Hello, " ++ name ++ "!") env.stdout
            )

name: Terminal
comment:
A program run from a terminal may want to colour its output, draw to the
size of the window, read single keypresses or set the window title. This
module tells it whether a terminal is there, how many colours it can show and
how big it is, and lets it switch stdin into raw mode, set the title and hear
about resizes.

A _terminal_ here is a standard stream connected to a terminal device rather
than to a file or a pipe. `configuration` and `setTitle` act on stdout, and
`setStdinRawMode` on stdin: `configuration` gives `Nothing` and the other two
do nothing when that stream is not a terminal. There is therefore no setup
step, and none of the tasks can fail. `configuration` is how a program finds
out whether stdout is a terminal.

On the native backend on Windows, running any of these tasks, or subscribing
with `onResize`, stops the program with a fatal error saying it is not
supported there yet.


## Configuration

@docs Configuration, Size, configuration


## Commands

@docs setStdinRawMode, setTitle


## Subscriptions

@docs onResize

aliases.name: Configuration
aliases.comment:
What is known about the terminal on stdout: how many colours it can show,
and the size of its window in character cells.

`colorDepth` is a number of bits per colour: `1` for no colour, `4` for 16
colours, `8` for 256 colours and `24` for true colour. It is not asked of the
terminal but guessed from the environment, by the first of these rules that
applies:

  - a non-empty `NO_COLOR`, or `TERM=dumb`, gives `1`;
  - `FORCE_COLOR` set to exactly `0`, `1`, `2` or `3` gives `1`, `4`, `8` or
    `24`;
  - `COLORTERM` set to `truecolor` or `24bit` gives `24`;
  - a `TERM` ending in `256color` gives `8`;
  - otherwise it is `4`.

The size is the one stdout reports or, when stdout reports a width of zero,
the one another standard stream that is a terminal reports (stdin, then
stderr, on the native backend; stderr on the JS backend). `columns` and `rows`
are both `0` when none can be read.
aliases.type: { colorDepth : Basics.Int, columns : Basics.Int, rows : Basics.Int }

aliases.name: Size
aliases.comment: The size of a terminal window, in character cells.
aliases.type: { columns : Basics.Int, rows : Basics.Int }

values.name: configuration
values.comment:
Gets the configuration of the terminal on stdout, or `Nothing` when stdout
is not a terminal, as when the output is redirected to a file or a pipe.

It reads the terminal again each time it is run, so a later run reports the
current size.

values.name: onResize
values.comment:
Creates a subscription to changes in the size of the terminal, with the new
size.

A size arrives each time the program receives `SIGWINCH`, the signal the
operating system sends when a terminal's window is resized, and may equal the
previous one. It is read as `configuration` reads its size, falling back to
the other standard streams also when stdout is not a terminal, and nothing
arrives when no standard stream reports one, or, on the native backend, when
the program is embedded in a host application. The subscription does not keep
the program running.

values.name: setStdinRawMode
values.comment:
Switches stdin into raw mode with `True`, and back to its original mode with
`False`. It does nothing when stdin is not a terminal.

In its original mode a terminal usually hands input over a line at a time,
once the user presses enter. In raw mode every keypress is sent over the stdin
stream as it happens, and is not echoed. Key combinations such as Ctrl-C arrive
as input too, rather than raising a signal, so `System.onSignalInterrupt` does
not see them.

The original mode is the one stdin had when this was first run. It is restored
when the process exits, but on the native backend not when a fatal error stops
the program. It is also restored when the program is ended by an interrupt
(`SIGINT`) or terminate (`SIGTERM`) signal it does not subscribe to, unless,
on the native backend, the program is embedded in a host application, which
keeps its own signal handling; any other signal that ends the program leaves
raw mode on. While the program subscribes to that signal
with `System.onSignalInterrupt` or `System.onSignalTerminate`, the signal does
not end it and raw mode stays on.

values.name: setTitle
values.comment:
Sets the title of the terminal window, as shown in the title bar or tab of a
terminal emulator.

It writes the title escape sequence (OSC 2) to stdout when stdout is a
terminal, and does nothing otherwise, so the sequence never ends up in a
redirected file or pipe. ASCII control characters, DEL included, are removed
from `title` first, so that none of them (BEL or ESC in particular) can end
the sequence early. Whether the title changes is up to the terminal, and a
failure to write is ignored.

name: WebSocket
comment:
A WebSocket (RFC 6455) is a full-duplex connection that carries messages rather than bytes
and is opened by an HTTP request, and this module opens WebSockets as a client and answers them
as a server.

A client [`connect`](#connect)s to a `ws://` or `wss://` URL. A server receives a client's
opening request as an [`Upgrade`](#Upgrade), either on a [`Socket.Connection`](Socket#Connection)
it accepted ([`receiveUpgrade`](#receiveUpgrade)) or from an HTTP server
([`Http.Server.upgradeRequest`](Http-Server#upgradeRequest)), and answers it with
[`accept`](#accept) or [`reject`](#reject). Either way an open connection is a
[`WebSocket`](#WebSocket).

    WebSocket.connect (WebSocket.defaultConnectOptions "wss://example.com/chat")
        |> Task.andThen
            (\ws ->
                Stream.write (WebSocket.Text "hello") (WebSocket.writable ws)
                    |> Task.mapError (\_ -> ...)
            )

Several modules define functions such as `close`, `accept` and `readable`, so import this module
qualified:

    import WebSocket

**Messages.** A message is text or binary data ([`Message`](#Message)). A connection is opened in
one of two _modes_, and its type says which. In the _whole_ mode ([`connect`](#connect),
[`accept`](#accept)) every message arrives in one piece, on [`readable`](#readable) or through
[`onMessage`](#onMessage), and a message larger than the `maxMessageSize` of its options fails
the connection. In the _streamed_ mode ([`connectStreamed`](#connectStreamed),
[`acceptStreamed`](#acceptStreamed)) every message arrives as a stream of its own
([`StreamedMessage`](#StreamedMessage)), whatever its size. A streamed message must be read to
its end (`Closed`) or cancelled, because the connection delivers nothing after it until then. In
both modes each value written to [`writable`](#writable) is one message, and
[`sendText`](#sendText) and [`sendBinary`](#sendBinary) send one message whose content is read
from a stream. While 1 MiB of received messages, or 1024 of them, wait unread, the connection
stops reading from the network.

**Ending.** A connection normally ends with a _closing handshake_: one end sends a Close frame
carrying a [`CloseCode`](#CloseCode) and a reason, the other answers with its own, and the
connection is then gone. This end can also _fail_ a connection, for example on a protocol error,
an invalid or oversized message, or a silent peer: it sends a Close frame with a code saying why
and closes the connection without waiting for an answer. And the network connection can simply
be lost. [`awaitClose`](#awaitClose) and [`onClose`](#onClose) report how a connection ended, as
a [`CloseInfo`](#CloseInfo).

The tasks of this module that can fail fail with this module's [`Error`](#Error), which holds
the failure of whichever layer failed: the connection underneath, TLS for `wss://`, or the
WebSocket itself. Once a connection is open, a failure of the connection arrives on its streams
instead, as the [`Stream`](Stream) module describes: a read of [`readable`](#readable) fails with
`Stream.Failed`, and [`fromStreamFailure`](#fromStreamFailure) reads that failure back as an
`Error`, such as [`ProtocolViolation`](#Error) when the peer broke the protocol.

**Liveness.** By default this end checks that the peer is still there: when nothing has arrived
for 30 seconds it sends a ping, and when still nothing at all has arrived 30 seconds later it
fails the connection ([`Heartbeat`](#Heartbeat)). Pings from the peer are answered until this
end starts closing.

**Compression.** permessage-deflate (RFC 7692) compresses the content of each message. By
default a client offers it and a server accepts the offer, both without _context takeover_: each
message is compressed on its own, without referring back to earlier ones. With
`contextTakeover = True` in the compression options of both sides a message may refer back into
earlier messages, which compresses a run of similar messages better. A message written to
[`writable`](#writable) that is shorter than the compression options' `threshold` bytes is sent
uncompressed, while a non-empty message sent with
[`sendText`](#sendText) or [`sendBinary`](#sendBinary) is compressed whatever its size.
[`compression`](#compression) tells what the handshake agreed. Do not send secrets and data an
attacker controls on one compressed connection: the compressed sizes can reveal the secrets (the
CRIME and BREACH attacks).

A connection keeps the program running while an [`onMessage`](#onMessage) subscription exists
and the connection is open, while an [`onClose`](#onClose) subscription waits for its
`CloseInfo`, while an [`awaitClose`](#awaitClose) waits, during a closing handshake this end
started, and while an operation on it, such as a read, a write or a [`ping`](#ping), is waiting.

**Client limits.** A client opens a new connection for every [`connect`](#connect), even to a
host it is already connecting to, although RFC 6455 asks a client to wait for one opening
handshake with a host to finish before it starts another. Redirects are not followed (a redirect
status fails the handshake), and no proxy is used.

On native Windows, WebSockets are not supported: connecting, receiving an opening request and
accepting one fail with [`SocketError`](#Error) of kind
[`Socket.NotSupported`](Socket#ErrorKind).
